[MUQATIL:1:5-7/r1] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | To worship God alone means to affirm His oneness, as the feminine participle in another verse means monotheists. | mentions 66:5
[MUQATIL:1:5-7/r2] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The servant asks God for help in carrying out worship.
[MUQATIL:1:5-7/r8] MUQATIL, d. 150 · أبو هريرة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A report from Abū Hurayra says the Prophet related that God divided this sūra between Himself and the servant: praise is thanks, the two mercy names are praise, the King verse is glorification, and the rest belongs to the servant; seeking help is God's special acknowledgment of the servant's plea.
[MAJAZ:v1p14/r9] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | The construction implies omitted prepositions: ‘to the path’ and ‘for the path.’
[MAJAZ:v1p22/r2] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | The direct address in iyyāka naʿbudu is evidence for the vocative accusative analysis.
[MAJAZ:v1p22/r4] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | After referring to the absent, the discourse returns to direct address in ‘You alone we worship, You alone we ask for help, guide us.’
[MAJAZ:v1p22/r6] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | The shift between absent and present address is illustrated by ʿAntara ibn Shaddād’s cited verse.
[MAJAZ:v1p22/r7] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Abū Kabīr al-Hudhalī’s cited address likewise illustrates a turn from speaking about someone to addressing them.
[MAJAZ:v1p22/r8] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Placing the object pronoun before the verb is grammatical; al-ʿAjjāj’s ‘iyyāka adʿū’ exemplifies the order.
[MAJAZ:v1p22/r9] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Putting the pronoun after a verb-first clause, as in adʿū iyyāka, is impossible, but adding it after the verb’s object suffix, adʿūka iyyāka, is allowed.
[AKHFASH:v1p15#2/r4] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | The shift to addressing God as iyyāka is by revelation: God instructs the Prophet to say the praise and then to say iyyāka naʿbudu.
[AKHFASH:v1p15#2/r5] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | Iyyāka is used instead of anta because the pronoun is an object of naʿbudu; object position takes ka, hi, or the iyyā form. | mentions 34:24, 17:67
[AKHFASH:v1p16/r1] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | Iyyāka in both naʿbudu and nastaʿīn is accusative as the object; nominative positions instead take forms such as anta, antum, huwa, or hiya.
[AKHFASH:v1p17/r6] AKHFASH, d. 215 · العرب | reports | Some Arabs say hiyyāka for iyyāka, treating the initial alif as h, like ih or hih and haraqtu for araqtu.
[AKHFASH:v1p3#2/r5] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | The same waṣl rule applies to initial alifs in verbs or verbal nouns whose imperfect form begins with a fatḥa vowel on its yāʾ, as in the cited imperatives. | mentions 1:5, 1:6, 2:16, 28:38, 38:42
[MUSNAD-AHMAD:7291/r1] MUSNAD-AHMAD, d. 241 · أبو هريرة عن النبي | reports | Abu Hurayra relates that the Prophet called a prayer without al-Fatiha defective and told a Persian worshipper to recite it.
[MUSNAD-AHMAD:7291/r2] MUSNAD-AHMAD, d. 241 · النبي | reports | In a divine report, God says the prayer is divided between Him and the servant; this verse is shared, and the servant receives what he asks in the following supplication. | mentions 1:1, 1:2, 1:7
[MUSNAD-AHMAD:7836/r1] MUSNAD-AHMAD, d. 241 · النبي | reports | God calls the opening praises acknowledgments from the servant, makes this verse the shared portion, and grants the servant's requests in the closing supplication. | mentions 1:1, 1:2, 1:7
[MUSNAD-AHMAD:7836/r2] MUSNAD-AHMAD, d. 241 · النبي | reports | The Prophet calls prayer without al-Fatiha incomplete; Abu Hurayra tells a worshipper behind the imam to recite it inwardly.
[MUSNAD-AHMAD:9932/r1] MUSNAD-AHMAD, d. 241 · النبي | reports | The divine report assigns the opening praise to God, this verse to both God and servant, and the requests in the final verses to the servant. | mentions 1:1, 1:2, 1:7
[MUSNAD-AHMAD:9932/r2] MUSNAD-AHMAD, d. 241 · النبي | reports | The Prophet says prayer without al-Fatiha is deficient; Abu Hurayra instructs a follower behind the imam to recite it to himself.
[TUSTARI:1:5#2/r1] TUSTARI, d. 283 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Abu Hurayra reports that when the imam says the final phrase, worshippers should say Amin; agreement with the angels' Amin brings forgiveness for past sins.
[TUSTARI:1:5/r1] TUSTARI, d. 283 · author | holds | Worship means submission, humility, confession of God's lordship, affirming His unity, and serving Him; the word servant derives from this sense.
[TUSTARI:1:5/r2] TUSTARI, d. 283 · author | holds | Seeking help asks God to enable sincere fulfillment of His obligations, since will, knowledge, sincerity, and all power depend on His support.
[TUSTARI:1:5/r3] TUSTARI, d. 283 · author | holds | Asking for guidance requests an increase in divine support and empowerment, even after God has already guided the servant. | mentions 50:35
[TUSTARI:1:5/r4] TUSTARI, d. 283 · author | holds | Another sense of guidance is direction to Islam, the path to God, through divine insight, since guidance comes only from Him. | mentions 28:22
[TUSTARI:1:5/r5] TUSTARI, d. 283 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A report from Thawban says prayer is divided between God and the servant: praise and glorification are for God, then the servant receives what he asks.
[TUSTARI:1:5/r6] TUSTARI, d. 283 · author | holds | Sahl explains God's saying He is praised as describing Him through abundant beneficence and generosity.
[TUSTARI:1:5/r7] TUSTARI, d. 283 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid reports that Amin is one of God's names.
[TUSTARI:1:5/r8] TUSTARI, d. 283 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says Christians envy Muslims for saying Amin.
[TUSTARI:1:5/r9] TUSTARI, d. 283 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A report from Jabir urges steadfastness despite its difficulty, calls prayer the best deed, and says saying Amin after the imam brings God's approval, accepted prayer, and answered supplication.
[TAB:1:2/r11] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | God speaks both clauses: He praises Himself, then teaches and obliges His servants to recite them as a test, with an understood command to say them signaled by “You alone we worship.” | mentions 1:5
[TAB:1:2/r12] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | The command “say” is omitted because Arabic speakers omit words recoverable from context; here the following worship clause reveals that the praise clause is also an instruction to servants. | mentions 1:5
[TAB:1:5/r1] TAB, d. 310 · author | prefers | Al-Tabari interprets “You alone we worship” as humbling, abasing, and submitting ourselves to God alone, acknowledging His lordship.
[TAB:1:5/r10] TAB, d. 310 · بعض أهل الغفلة | reports | Some inattentive readers took the verse as an instance of fronting and delaying the intended order, like Imruʾ al-Qays's line about enough money and seeking more.
[TAB:1:5/r11] TAB, d. 310 · author | rejects | Al-Tabari rejects the delayed-order analogy: having enough money does not prevent seeking more, whereas worship and divine aid entail one another, so their stated order is sound.
[TAB:1:5/r12] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | The fronted object pronoun is repeated with each verb because each verb governs its own object; Arabic speech is more eloquent when the object is repeated, though omission is permissible when the pronoun follows the verb.
[TAB:1:5/r13] TAB, d. 310 · بعض من لم يمعن النظر | reports | Some who did not examine closely compared the repeated “You alone” to the repeated “between” in verses by ʿAdī ibn Zayd and al-Aʿshā of Hamdān.
[TAB:1:5/r14] TAB, d. 310 · author | rejects | Al-Tabari rejects the analogy: “between” requires two complements and is incomplete when one is omitted, but “You alone we worship” is already a complete clause, and each verb properly takes the repeated object.
[TAB:1:5/r2] TAB, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbas reports Gabriel's gloss that worship means to affirm God's oneness, fear Him, and hope in Him alone.
[TAB:1:5/r3] TAB, d. 310 · author | prefers | Al-Tabari prefers humility and submission to fear and hope because worship in Arabic fundamentally means abasement; the road called muʿabbad is trodden and subdued, as in Ṭarafa's verse, and a ridden camel is also muʿabbad.
[TAB:1:5/r4] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | The servants seek God's aid for worship, obedience, and all their affairs, relying on no one else, unlike disbelievers who seek aid from the idols they worship.
[TAB:1:5/r5] TAB, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbas glosses the request as seeking God's aid for obedience and all one's affairs.
[TAB:1:5/r6] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | The believer asks for help with obedience during the remaining life, not past deeds; God's enabling of the limbs and gift of guidance are grace, not an obligation, and granting or withholding aid entails neither injustice nor faulty governance.
[TAB:1:5/r7] TAB, d. 310 · القائلين بالتفويض من أهل القدر | rejects | Al-Tabari rejects the Qadari delegation claim that God may command a duty only after making its performance and omission possible through necessary aid; the verse teaches believers to ask for assistance as a divine favor.
[TAB:1:5/r8] TAB, d. 310 · author | rejects | He argues that the Qadari premise makes asking for aid equivalent to asking God not to act unjustly, but Muslims approve the former supplication and reject the latter, exposing the premise's error.
[TAB:1:5/r9] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Worship precedes the request for aid because each entails the other: a servant cannot worship without God's aid, and aid for worship is realized in the servant's act; either order conveys the relation.
[TAB:1:7/r54] TAB, d. 310 · أهل الإلحاد الطاعنون في القرآن | reports | Critics ask why al-Fātiḥa has seven verses when, they argue, the meaning of its remaining verses is already contained in “Master of Judgment Day” and “You alone we worship and ask for help.”

uthor | holds | Earlier scriptures each contain some meanings found together in the Qur'an: the Torah gives admonitions and detail, the Psalms praise and glorify, and the Gospel admonishes and reminds; the Qur'an gathers these and adds more.
[TAB:1:7/r56] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Ṭabarī says the prior books lack a miracle certifying their recipients, whereas the Qur'an's unmatched composition defeats all attempts to produce even a short surah and proves Muhammad's prophethood.
[TAB:1:7/r57] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | The Qur'an's varied contents—encouragement, warning, commands, prohibitions, stories, argument, and parables—also make its extended expression purposeful.
[TAB:1:7/r58] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Fātiḥa's inimitable arrangement proves prophethood, while its praise and glorification direct people to recognize God's greatness, sovereignty, power, and dominion and to thank Him for His favors.
[TAB:1:7/r59] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | The account of those favored through knowledge of God and His enabling teaches that every religious and worldly blessing comes from Him, directing requests to God rather than idols or rivals.
[TAB:1:7/r60] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Recounting punishments for disobedience warns people away from sin and from incurring God's anger, whose consequences lead to destruction.
[TAB:1:7/r61] TAB, d. 310 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Abū Hurayra reports that the Prophet said God answers the worshipper's recitation: He calls al-ḥamdu praise, al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm commendation, Mālik Yawm al-Dīn glorification, and the rest of the surah the servant's share.
[TAB:1:7/r62] TAB, d. 310 · أبو هريرة | reports | A second Abū Hurayra version gives the same recitation exchange but is not attributed to the Prophet.
[TAB:1:7/r63] TAB, d. 310 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh reports the divine saying that the prayer is divided between God and His servant, with the servant receiving what he asks; the first three praises are God's, and what follows is for the servant.
[TAB-FULL:v1p155/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | rejects | Ṭabarī says the accusative is unnecessary: revelation commands Muhammad to say both the descriptions of God and then the direct address, and Arabic allows this shift within reported speech. | mentions 1:2, 1:3, 1:5
[TAB-FULL:v1p157/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Poetry by Abū Kabīr al-Hudhalī and Labīd, and Qurʾān 10:22, show that Arabic can move from third-person report to direct address without requiring a vocative construction. | mentions 10:22, 1:5
[TAB-FULL:v1p159/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | prefers | The worship clause means humbling, submitting, and lowering ourselves to God in acknowledgment of His lordship, exclusively; al-Ṭabarī prefers this sense to fear and hope because servitude is rooted in abasement.
[TAB-FULL:v1p159/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas reports Gabriel's gloss to Muhammad: worship means affirming God's oneness, fearing and hoping in Him alone.
[TAB-FULL:v1p159/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Arabic calls a road trodden and subdued by feet maʿbad, and a camel subdued for errands maʿbad; the servant's name reflects subjection to its master, supporting worship as abasement.
[TAB-FULL:v1p161/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The supplication seeks God's help alone for worship, obedience, and every affair; unlike idolaters who seek aid from their idols, believers serve God sincerely.
[TAB-FULL:v1p161/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas glosses the request as seeking God's help in obeying Him and in all affairs.
[TAB-FULL:v1p161/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Help is requested for the remaining lifetime and future obedience, not completed past deeds; enabling the limbs and granting success are divine favor and لطف, whose unequal bestowal is neither mismanagement nor injustice.
[TAB-FULL:v1p161/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | rejects | The prayer for help refutes Qadariyyah proponents of tafwīḍ, who claim God must grant each commanded person the assistance needed to act or refrain; otherwise asking help would amount to asking God not to commit injustice.
[TAB-FULL:v1p161/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Worship may precede the request for help because worship and its enabling aid necessarily accompany one another, like saying either that someone fulfilled a need and thereby helped, or helped and thereby fulfilled it.
[TAB-FULL:v1p161/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | rejects | He rejects the suggestion that the sequence uses a fronted phrase whose intended meaning comes later, a proposal attributed to some inattentive readers and illustrated by Imruʾ al-Qays.
[TAB-FULL:v1p163/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | rejects | The Imruʾ al-Qays analogy fails: having enough money does not entail giving up desire for more, whereas worship and the aid enabling it necessarily coexist, so their order is not semantic reversal.
[TAB-FULL:v1p163/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The repeated second-person object is idiomatic and more eloquent: Arabic repeats a pronoun with each verb, whether attached after the verb or fronted within iyyāka, though omission is possible when attached.
[TAB-FULL:v1p163/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · بعض من لم يمعن النظر | reports | Some inattentive readers compare the repeated iyyāka before nastaʿīn to paired repetitions in poetic expressions such as between one person and another.
[TAB-FULL:v1p164/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | rejects | The analogy to paired phrases with bayna is mistaken: bayna requires two complements, so omitting one makes the sentence defective, while iyyāka nعبد is already a complete clause.
[TAB-FULL:v1p164/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Each clause independently needs its object pronoun, just as every verb may repeat its attached object; therefore iyyāka properly recurs before nastaʿīn.
[TAB-FULL:v1p199/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Answering why al-Fātiḥa has seven verses if two contain its meanings: earlier scriptures each included only some meanings, while the Qur'an gathers all of them for Muhammad's community and adds many more.
[TAB-FULL:v1p199/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The Torah is admonition and detailed instruction, Psalms praise and glorification, and Gospel admonition and reminder, but none has a miracle proving its recipient; the Qur'an contains these meanings and more.
[TAB-FULL:v1p199/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Among the Qur'an's distinctive merits is its miraculous arrangement and composition: rhetoricians cannot compose even a sura as short as one of its chapters.
[TAB-FULL:v1p203/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · أبو هريرة عن رسول الله | reports | The Prophet reports God praises the servant’s recitation of praise, mercy, and sovereignty, then says the invocation from You alone we worship through the end belongs to the servant. | mentions 1:2, 1:1, 1:4, 1:5
[ZAJJAJ:v1p47/r4] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | ʿIbāda means obedience together with humility; the phrase means that we obey God with submission.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p47/r5] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | A road is called maʿbad when much foot traffic has subdued it, and a camel is maʿbad when coated with tar.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p47/r6] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Iyyāka is the accusative object, while its kāf is genitive through annexation to iyyā; iyyā is a noun used for accusative pronouns and may take any such pronoun.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p47/r7] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Adding iyyā to an overt noun, as in iyyā Zayd, is inelegant because it is reserved for pronouns.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p47/r8] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl transmits an Arab expression warning a man over sixty to beware of young women, with iyyā used before a noun.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p47/r9] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | rejects | He rejects the claim that iyyāka is one indivisible noun: nouns do not take annexation this way, while Arabic treats the hāʾ of iyyāhu like that in ʿaṣāhu.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p49/r1] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Nastaʿīnu originally was nastaʿūnu, from maʿūna and ʿawn; wāw became yāʾ under the weight of kasra, the kasra moved to ʿayn, and the resulting sound changes follow examples like aʿāna/yaʿīnu.
[IBNABIHATIM:v1p29#2/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says Gabriel commanded Muhammad to say that God alone is worshipped, unified, feared, and hoped in, with no other lord.
[IBNABIHATIM:v1p29#2/r2] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · قتادة | reports | Qatada says the wording itself indicates God's exclusive claim: worshippers should say it as instructed.
[IBNABIHATIM:v1p29#2/r3] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · قتادة | reports | Qatada says God commands sincere worship and asks people to seek His help in their affairs.
[IBNABIHATIM:v1p29#2/r4] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says help is sought for obedience to God and for all one's affairs.
[NAHHAS:v1p171/r10] NAHHAS, d. 338 · الفضل بن عيسى الرقاشي | reports | Al-Faḍl ibn ʿĪsā al-Raqāshī reads iyyāka with fatḥa on the hamza.
[NAHHAS:v1p171/r11] NAHHAS, d. 338 · عمرو بن فائد | reports | ʿAmr ibn Fāʾid reads iyyāka in a shortened form.
[NAHHAS:v1p171/r12] NAHHAS, d. 338 · الخليل وسيبويه | reports | Al-Khalīl and Sībawayh treat iyā as the noun and the attached kāf as genitive; the Kufans treat iyyāka as one complete noun.
[NAHHAS:v1p171/r13] NAHHAS, d. 338 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl calls iyā a pronoun; Abū al-ʿAbbās objects that pronouns are not annexed and calls it an ambiguous expression like kull.
[NAHHAS:v1p171/r14] NAHHAS, d. 338 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl says naʿbudu is indicative because it resembles nouns.
[NAHHAS:v1p171/r15] NAHHAS, d. 338 · سيبويه | reports | Sībawayh says the imperfect is indicative because it resembles nouns.
[NAHHAS:v1p171/r16] NAHHAS, d. 338 · الكسائي | reports | Al-Kisāʾī says the imperfect is indicative because of its prefixes.
[NAHHAS:v1p171/r17] NAHHAS, d. 338 · الفراء | reports |

 Al-Farrāʾ says the imperfect is indicative because it is free of jussive and subjunctive particles.
[NAHHAS:v1p171/r18] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | Iyyāka is also the object of nastaʿīn, and the two clauses are coordinated.
[NAHHAS:v1p171/r19] NAHHAS, d. 338 · يحيى بن وثاب والأعمش | reports | Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb and al-Aʿmash read nastaʿīn with kasra on the nūn, a Tamīm, Asad, Qays, and Rabīʿa usage.
[NAHHAS:v1p171/r20] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | The form derives from istaʿwana: the wāw shifts its vowel to the preceding consonant and becomes yāʾ; istiʿāna similarly derives from istiʿwān, with a compensatory tāʾ after a long vowel is deleted.
[IBNHIBBAN:1784/r1] IBNHIBBAN, d. 354 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet calls a prayer without Umm al-Qur'an deficient and incomplete.
[IBNHIBBAN:1784/r2] IBNHIBBAN, d. 354 · أبو هريرة | reports | Abu Hurayra advises the man who prays behind an imam to recite the Fatiha quietly to himself.

[IBNHIBBAN:1795/r2] IBNHIBBAN, d. 354 · أبو هريرة | reports | Abu Hurayra tells a follower behind the imam to recite the Fatiha inwardly.

[IBNHIBBAN:776/r3] IBNHIBBAN, d. 354 · الله تبارك وتعالى | reports | The hadith divides the prayer between God and the servant: this verse is their shared exchange, while the remaining request for guidance belongs to the servant. | mentions 1:2, 1:1, 1:7
[IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p39/r1] IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB, d. 392 · الفضل الرقاشي | reports | Al-Faḍl al-Raqqāshī reads the pronoun with initial hamza opened; Ibn Jinnī treats this as a recognized dialectal variant, also heard with initial hāʾ.
[IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p39/r2] IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB, d. 392 · عمرو بن فايد | reports | ʿAmr b. Fāʾid lightens the doubled yāʾ in both pronouns; Ibn Jinnī analyzes īyā as faʿl, like riḍā, and links it with the word for the sun’s ray or sign.
[IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p39/r3] IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB, d. 392 · author | reports | Abū Isḥāq glosses the address as worshipping God’s reality, deriving īyā from āya, ‘sign’; Ibn Jinnī says this derivation works only on Abū Isḥāq’s view that īyā is a special name for the pronoun.
[IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p39/r4] IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB, d. 392 · author | rejects | Ibn Jinnī rejects treating the lightened pronunciation as an established dialect: he finds no linguistic record for it and suspects ʿAmr reduced the yāʾs to avoid their heaviness.
[IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p39/r5] IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB, d. 392 · author | holds | The cited verses of Ṭarafa and Dhū al-Rumma use iyā/iyāʾ for sunlight, supporting the form’s association with the sun’s visible sign.
[IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p40/r1] IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB, d. 392 · author | holds | Arabic has other attested lightening and consonant changes, illustrated by al-Farazdaq and other verse; Ibn Jinnī still says the Qurʾān should not adopt the unattested lightening of īyā.
[SULAMI:v1p36#4/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · author | holds | Worship is sincere action without attachments or compensation; one seeks God's help to remain in that state because worship is through Him, not oneself.
[SULAMI:v1p36#4/r10] SULAMI, d. 412 · author | holds | Worship is by direct witnessing, while divine help is sought for affliction.
[SULAMI:v1p36#4/r11] SULAMI, d. 412 · الجنيد | reports | Those granted knowledge of servanthood first devote worship to God, then recognize that He alone enables and helps them give thanks for worship.
[SULAMI:v1p36#4/r12] SULAMI, d. 412 · القاسم | reports | Worship is by divine enablement, and help is sought to thank God for enabling it.
[SULAMI:v1p36#4/r13] SULAMI, d. 412 · أبو جعفر الفرغلي | reports | Whoever affirms the verse is absolved of both determinism and the opposing doctrine of human self-determination.
[SULAMI:v1p36#4/r2] SULAMI, d. 412 · author | holds | The paired clauses can mean worship with sincerity and seeking help to unveil one's secrets.
[SULAMI:v1p36#4/r3] SULAMI, d. 412 · author | holds | Another reading pairs worship through intention with divine aid in aspiration.
[SULAMI:v1p36#4/r4] SULAMI, d. 412 · author | holds | One worships through knowledge and seeks help for gnosis.
[SULAMI:v1p36#4/r5] SULAMI, d. 412 · author | holds | True worship recognizes that God enabled it; divine help is needed for its acceptance and correction.
[SULAMI:v1p36#4/r6] SULAMI, d. 412 · author | holds | Worship is performed by God's command and depends on His grace.
[SULAMI:v1p36#4/r7] SULAMI, d. 412 · author | holds | The servant asks to be freed from spiritual claims and carried from them into the gardens of realities.
[SULAMI:v1p36#4/r8] SULAMI, d. 412 · author | holds | Worship is outward and reliance inward; repeating You removes the perception that either worship or reliance belongs to the self.
[SULAMI:v1p36#4/r9] SULAMI, d. 412 · author | holds | The prayer asks God to qualify, purify, and aid worshippers while protecting them from self-regard about their worship.
[THALABI:v1p103/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | In the divine report dividing prayer between God and the servant, the basmala glorifies God, al-ḥamdu praises Him, al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm extols Him, Mālik delegates the matter, the worship-and-help verse is shared, and guidance is granted to the servant.
[THALABI:v1p117/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The verse shifts from third-person report to direct address, an instance of rhetorical turn; another analysis supplies the omitted command “say: You alone.”
[THALABI:v1p117/r10] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The author glosses worship as affirming oneness, devoting oneself sincerely, obeying, and submitting; it is disciplining the self to bear hardship in obedience and originally means humility and submission.
[THALABI:v1p117/r11] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The Arabic root of worship connotes humility and being trodden down, as in a leveled path; Ṭarafa’s verse supplies poetic evidence.
[THALABI:v1p117/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Iyyāka is an object-case pronoun, with the kāf in a genitive relation to the pronoun; its attachment to a pronoun is illustrated by poetry and ordinary speech.
[THALABI:v1p117/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl reports that Arabs say “iyyāhu wa-iyyākum” when a man reaches sixty.
[THALABI:v1p117/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Iyyāka normally precedes the verb, as in “You I mean”; after the verb it occurs only under restriction, as in “I worship none but You.”
[THALABI:v1p117/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو ميثم سهل بن محمد | reports | Abū Maytham classifies pronouns as attached, detached, or implicit, giving examples of each and explaining their labels.
[THALABI:v1p117/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو زيد | reports | Abū Zayd analyzes iyyā as two yāʾs, one relational and one vocative, originally ay yā and merged.
[THALABI:v1p117/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو عبيد | reports | Abū ʿUbayd derives iyyāka from awyāka, with wāw changed to yāʾ, connecting it to seeking refuge and turning toward an aim.
[THALABI:v1p117/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · الفضل الرقاشي | reports | Al-Faḍl al-Raqāshī reads the first alif of iyyāka with fatḥa, describing it as a dialect form.
[THALABI:v1p117/r9] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The fronted object is clearer and rhetorically better than naʿbuduka because attention turns from the worship to God, not from the worshiper toward the act.
[THALABI:v1p118/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | A camel described as maʿbad is coated with tar; Ṭarafa's verse illustrates the usage.
[THALABI:v1p118/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The word ʿabd reflects a servant's abasement and submission to his master.
[THALABI:v1p118/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Seeking help means asking aid for worship and for all one's affairs.
[THALABI:v1p118/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · الفراء | reports | Yaḥyā ibn Riʾāb reads نستعين with a kasra; al-Farrāʾ says several tribes kasrate future markers except yāʾ, while Quraysh and Kināna open them, the more eloquent and common form.
[THALABI:v1p118/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Repeating إياك strengthens sincerity, exclusivity, and emphasis; the author adduces repeated phrasing in scripture and poetry. | mentions 20:33, 20:34
[THALABI:v1p118/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو بكر الوراق | reports | Worship is owed because God created people, and help is sought because God guided them.
[THALABI:v1p118/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو الحسن علي بن عبد الرحمن الفران | reports | Al-Farrān gives several paired reasons: God is maker and people made, worship earns Paradise, help averts Fire, people are servants and God generous, and God alone is truly worshipped.
[MAWARDI:1:5/r1] MAWARDI, d. 450 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalil says the divine name is annexed to the pronoun kaf in iyyaka.
[MAWARDI:1:5/r2] MAWARDI, d. 450 · الأخفش | reports | Al-Akhfash takes iyyaka as a single pronoun for God, not an annexation, because a pronoun is not annexed.
[MAWARDI:1:5/r3] MAWARDI, d. 450 · author | prefers | The clearest sense of worship is humility, the highest form of submission, owed only to God as giver of the greatest g

[MAWARDI:1:5/r4] MAWARDI, d. 450 · unattributed | reports | A second interpretation takes worship to mean obedience.
[MAWARDI:1:5/r5] MAWARDI, d. 450 · unattributed | reports | A third interpretation takes worship to mean drawing near through obedience.
[MAWARDI:1:5/r6] MAWARDI, d. 450 · author | holds | Humility is clearest because Christians worshipped Jesus without obeying him through worship, while the Prophet is obeyed but is not thereby worshipped.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p57#2/r1] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · الخليل | reports | He parses iyyaka as God's name annexed to the second-person suffix kāf.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p57#2/r2] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · الأخفش | reports | He parses iyyaka as one word used as a pronoun for God, since a pronoun cannot be annexed.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p57#2/r3] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | One meaning of worship is submission, the highest form of submission, due only to the giver of greatest blessings such as life and the senses.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p57#2/r4] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | A second definition of worship is obedience.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p57#2/r5] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | A third definition of worship is drawing near through obedience.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p57#2/r6] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | prefers | The submission definition is clearest: Christians worshiped Jesus without obeying him, while the Prophet is obeyed but is not an object of worship.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p505#2/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl analyzes iyyā as a pronoun with kāf attached in genitive; Abū ʿUthmān is also said to hold this view.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p505#2/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو الحسن | reports | Abū al-Ḥasan treats iyyā itself as a pronoun whose ending changes with the number and person addressed; kāf merely marks address, as in dhālika.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p505#2/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو الحسن | reports | According to the transmitted account, Abū al-Ḥasan disallows combinations such as iyyā-ka with iyyā of Zayd or falsehood.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p505#2/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · سيبويه | reports | Sibawayh reports hearing an Arab say that after sixty a man should beware of himself and young women.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p505#2/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن كيسان | reports | Ibn Kaysān attributes to some grammarians the view that the full form iyyāka is a noun; others take its final yāʾ, kāf, or hāʾ as the pronoun and iyyā as support.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p505#2/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو إسحاق | reports | Abū Isḥāq says kāf is genitive by adding it to iyyā, which can also take the other attached pronouns.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p505#2/r7] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | prefers | The author accepts only Abū al-Ḥasan's account: a pronoun is already maximally definite and has no need for the specificity of annexation.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p505#2/r8] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | rejects | The author rejects the full-word analysis as weak: like anta, iyyā is the pronoun, while the kāf's vowel marks masculine or feminine address.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p511/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Pronouns divide into independent, attached, and hidden forms; they may be nominative, accusative, or genitive, though genitive pronouns have no independent form.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p511/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | A hidden pronoun is understood in a verb such as sat or stood because a verb cannot stand without a subject.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p511/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Iyyā is built on sukūn because it resembles a particle; its final alif is original, like the alifs in lā, mā, ḥattā, and kallā.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p511/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو إسحاق | reports | Abū Isḥāq reportedly glosses iyyā-ka naʿbud as we worship Your reality and derives iyyā from āya, a sign.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p511/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو الفتح | rejects | Abū al-Fatḥ rejects that derivation: pronouns are built forms, not derived words; since iyyā is a pronoun it should not be considered derived.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p511/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · صاحب النظم | reports | The author of al-Naẓm explains iyyā as exclusivity: iyyā-ka ḍarabtu directs the act specifically to you, which also explains its use in warnings such as beware the lion.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p516/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Worship is obedience joined to submission and humility, a form of abasement due only to God; ʿabd reflects a servant's lowliness and a well-trodden road is muʿabbad.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p516/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو بكر | reports | Abū Bakr says iyyā-ka is repeated for emphasis, like repeating bayna in the phrase between Zayd and ʿAmr.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p516/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو بكر | reports | He also notes that each verb independently selects an object: if placed after the verbs the phrase would be naʿbuduka wa-nastaʿīnuka, and both take the fronted iyyā-ka.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p516/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | prefers | The author prefers emphasis as the reason for repeating iyyā-ka, since Arabic can leave the shared object unspoken after the first coordinated verb.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p516/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The omitted object in 93:3, mā qalā, means mā qalāka and illustrates that coordination can share an object without repeating it. | mentions 93:3
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p516/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Putting worship before asking for help does not establish chronological order: the conjunction wāw joins things without requiring sequence.
[WAHIDI-QT:1:5/r1] WAHIDI-QT, d. 468 · author | holds | Worship is obedience with submission; worship is reserved for God alone, and help is sought from Him.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:1:5-7/r1] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | Worship means singling God out and directing oneself to Him in obedience joined with humility.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:1:5-7/r2] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | The worshippers ask God alone for help.
[JISHUMI:v1p210/r3] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The common reading has kasra on the first vowel of iyyāka and fatḥa on the first nūn of nastaʿīn; another Arabic dialect is possible but not an accepted reading.
[JISHUMI:v1p210/r4] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Iyyāka is derived as iwyāka, with wāw changed and assimilated into yāʾ, and is associated with seeking refuge; as a detached pronoun it precedes its verb unless a separator intervenes.
[JISHUMI:v1p210/r5] JISHUMI, d. 494 · أبو حاتم | reports | Abū Ḥātim classifies iyyāka as a detached pronoun, as opposed to connected or implicit pronouns.
[JISHUMI:v1p213/r1] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The second kind of divine assistance brings a person closer to doing a duty or choosing it, as with divine لطف; it belongs to one known to have such help and may precede or accompany action.
[JISHUMI:v1p213/r2] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Though assistance from God is obligatory in this account, asking for it remains meaningful: one who knows an act is good wants help to do it, and supplication can itself be worship or a لطف occasioned by the request.
[BAGHAWI:1:5/r1] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · author | holds | Iyyā is a pronoun used with an attached object pronoun before a verb, while after the verb it occurs only detached, as in “I intended only you.”
[BAGHAWI:1:5/r2] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · author | holds | “We worship” means we affirm God's oneness and obey Him humbly; worship is obedience with humility and submission, as a slave is compliant and a road is leveled.
[BAGHAWI:1:5/r3] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · author | holds | “We seek help” asks God to aid us in worship and in all our affairs.
[BAGHAWI:1:5/r4] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · author | holds | The question why worship precedes seeking aid matters to those who place ability before action; Baghawi says divine enabling and aid accompany the act, so the order makes no difference.
[BAGHAWI:1:5/r5] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · author | reports | Another explanation says seeking aid is itself a kind of worship, so the verse gives the general act of worship before one of its details.
[BAGHAWI:1:7/r36] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | In a qudsi report, God divides prayer between Himself and His servant and answers each part of al-Fatiha; Baghawi grades it sahih. | mentions 1:4
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p53#2/r1] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | Iyyaka is a pronoun used before a verb, as in ‘you alone I mean’; after a verb it appears only independently, as in ‘I meant only you.’
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p53#2/r2] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | Worship means making God one, obeying him with humility and submission; the word for servant reflects submission, as in a trodden path.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p53#2/r3] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | Seeking help asks God’s aid for worship and all affairs; the order is challenged by those who require capacity before action, but al-Baghawi says divine enabling accompanies action.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p53#2/r4] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | prefers | Because aid is itself a kind of worship, the verse can state worship generally and then name one of its details; on his view, the ordering poses no problem.
[KASHSHAF:1:5/r1] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | holds | Iya is a separate accusative pronoun; suffixes mark address, absence, and speaker without independent syntactic position.
[KASHSHAF:1:5/r10] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | holds | Worship is reserved for God because He gives the greatest blessings and deserves highest submission.
[KASHSHAF:1:5/r11] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | holds | The shift from third-person to address is iltifat; the Quran also shifts in 10:22 and 35:9. | mentions 10:22, 35:9
[KASHSHAF:1:5/r12] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · امرؤ القيس | reports | Imru al-Qays shifts perspective three times over three lines, illustrating varied discourse mode.
[KASHSHAF:1:5/r13] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | holds | Changing discourse mode refreshes attention and awakens listening; this placement has additional benefits.

[KASHSHAF:1:5/r14] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | holds | After praising God and listing His attributes, the speech directly addresses the one worthy of worship and help.
[KASHSHAF:1:5/r15] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | holds | Worship and help are paired to join what servants offer their Lord with what they request from Him.
[KASHSHAF:1:5/r16] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | holds | Worship comes before asking for help because offering the means before the request merits a response.
[KASHSHAF:1:5/r17] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | holds | Seeking help is unqualified so it covers every matter in which help is needed.
[KASHSHAF:1:5/r18] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | prefers | Best is asking God and His enabling grace for help in worship; 1:6 specifies aid as guidance. | mentions 1:6
[KASHSHAF:1:5/r19] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | holds | The request for guidance explains what help is sought and coheres with the preceding words. | mentions 1:6
[KASHSHAF:1:5/r2] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · الأخفش والمحققون | reports | Al-Akhfash and careful grammarians hold that suffixes are not independent pronouns, like the kاف in araʾaytaka.
[KASHSHAF:1:5/r20] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · ابن حبيش | reports | Ibn Hubaysh reads nastaʿinu with kasra on its initial nūn.
[KASHSHAF:1:5/r3] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · الخليل وبعض العرب | rejects | Al-Khalil reports an anomalous expression using iya without a suffix, which al-Zamakhshari says should not be relied on.
[KASHSHAF:1:5/r4] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | holds | Fronting the object gives exclusive force, as in 39:64 and 6:164. | mentions 39:64, 6:164
[KASHSHAF:1:5/r5] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | holds | The speakers devote worship and request help exclusively to God, seeking neither from anyone else.
[KASHSHAF:1:5/r6] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | reports | A reading weakens the yā in iyaaka.
[KASHSHAF:1:5/r7] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | reports | Another reading has fatḥa on the hamza and a geminated yā.
[KASHSHAF:1:5/r8] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · طفيل الغنوي | reports | A reading changes initial hamza to hāʾ; Tufayl al-Ghanawi's verse witnesses hiyyaka.
[KASHSHAF:1:5/r9] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | holds | Worship is utmost submission and abasement; related ʿabada describes thick, strongly woven cloth.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p55#2/r1] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · الأخفش | reports | Al-Akhfash and the verified grammarians treat the attached kāf, hā, and yā on iyya as markers of address, absence, or speech, not inflected pronouns.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p55#2/r2] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Putting the object first expresses exclusivity: worship and the request for help are directed to God alone. | mentions 39:64, 6:164
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p55#2/r3] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | reports | The reading has variants in the yā, hamza, and initial letter; Tufayl's verse witnesses the hā form.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p55#2/r4] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Worship is the utmost submission and humility, reserved for God because He is the giver of the greatest blessings.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p55#2/r5] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The shift from third-person praise to direct address is rhetorical iltifat; the explanation of its purpose continues in the next segment.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p56/r1] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Iltifat shifts among speech styles, as Quranic examples and Imru al-Qays's three successive shifts show; changing style renews attention and can carry special benefits. | mentions 10:22, 35:9
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p56/r2] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Direct address here makes the one already described as worthy of praise vivid, so worship and help are confined to the God whose qualities make Him deserving. | mentions 1:2
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p56/r3] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Joining worship with help unites what servants offer in drawing near to God with what they need from Him.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p56/r4] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Worship comes first because presenting a means before making a request makes a response more likely.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p56/r5] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The request for help is general, but its best sense is seeking God's aid and enabling grace to perform worship; the next verse specifies that request. | mentions 1:6
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p57/r1] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The request for guidance explains the help being sought: when asked how He should assist, the servants answer, guide us to the straight path.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p57/r2] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · ابن حبيش | reports | Ibn Hubaysh reads nasta'in with kasra on the initial nūn.
[IBNATIYYA:1:5/r1] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | holds | The believer's declaration confesses God's lordship, expresses humility, and affirms worship of God, unlike people who worship idols.
[IBNATIYYA:1:5/r10] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · بعضهم | reports | Another analysis treats kāf, hāʾ, and yāʾ as the pronouns, unable to stand alone; iyā supports them before verbs while suffixes attach directly after them.
[IBNATIYYA:1:5/r11] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · بعضهم | reports | A further view takes iyā as an ambiguous accusative pronoun base; its suffixes distinguish addressee, absent person, and speaker and have no syntactic case of their own.
[IBNATIYYA:1:5/r12] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | holds | Naʿbudu means to uphold the law and commands with humility and submission; maʿbad likewise names a smoothed path or camel.
[IBNATIYYA:1:5/r13] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · طرفة | reports | Ṭarafa's phrase “over a smoothed path” supports the lexical sense of maʿbad as something made smooth.
[IBNATIYYA:1:5/r14] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | holds | Iyyāka is repeated because the two different verbs each need emphasis and focused attention.
[IBNATIYYA:1:5/r15] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | holds | Nastaʿīnu means asking God for help in all affairs; the declaration as a whole disavows idols.
[IBNATIYYA:1:5/r16] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · الأعمش وابن وثاب والنخعي | reports | Al-Aʿmash, Ibn Waththāb, and al-Nakhaʿī read wa-nistaʿīnu with kasra on the initial nūn, a dialect of some Qurashīs.
[IBNATIYYA:1:5/r17] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | holds | The kasra dialect affects nūn, tāʾ, and hamza, not third-person yāʾ; it occurs with prefixed forms and certain Form I verbs, including hollow verbs.
[IBNATIYYA:1:5/r18] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | holds | In nastaʿīnu, the vowel of the original wāw moves to ʿayn, and the wāw becomes yāʾ because the preceding consonant has kasra.
[IBNATIYYA:1:5/r19] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | holds | The verbal noun istiʿāna derives from istiʿwānan: the wāw's vowel moves to ʿayn, then the wāw becomes alif after fatḥa.
[IBNATIYYA:1:5/r2] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | holds | The object is placed before the verb for emphasis and importance, following the Arabic tendency to put what matters first.
[IBNATIYYA:1:5/r20] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · بعضهم | reports | One analysis deletes the second of the two adjacent quiescent alifs because it was added for grammatical meaning and is more expendable.

[RAZI-FULL:v1p202/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Rationally, contingent beings receive existence and every perfection through God's creative power; thus every honor, joy, and virtue comes through servitude, the key to all good.

[RAZI-FULL:v1p204#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The worshiper asks God alone, not Gabriel or Michael, following Abraham's refusal of Gabriel's offer while tied by Nimrod and his trust that God knows his state; Rāzī compares his own helplessness before Hell and God's promised rescue. | mentions 21:69

[RAZI-FULL:v1p204/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Rāzī divides the case for reliance on God into rational proofs and transmitted evidence, then begins with the rational proofs.

[RAZI-FULL:v1p214#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The seven Fatiha verses remove seven vices: praise dispels desire, Lord of the worlds greed, Judgment Day anger, worship and aid pride and vanity, guidance caprice, the favored path unbelief and doubt, and the final phrase innovation.

[RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الله تعالى | reports | In a divine report transmitted by the Prophet, God responds to each Fatiha phrase: the opening remembers Him, praise praises Him, the mercy names magnify Him, Judgment Day glorifies Him or is entrusted to Him, worship belongs to Him, aid relies on Him, and guidance is the servant's request.

[RAZI-FULL:v1p218#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | prefers | The report that worship and aid belong between God and servant expresses determinism: a balanced capacity acts only when a decisive motive tips it, and that motive must be created by God.

[RAZI-FULL:v1p219/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The seven Fatiha verses correspond to the seven bodily prayer acts—standing, bowing, rising, first prostration, rising between prostrations, second prostration, and sitting—as soul to body.

[RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي | reports | A prophetic report says God has seventy veils of light; if unveiled, the splendor of His face would burn everything perceived by sight, and only prophetic light reveals the number.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Prayer was given to Muhammad as a gift for his community because it joins bodily ascent through actions with spiritual ascent through remembrances.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Before beginning the ascent, the worshipper purifies body and clothing for the holy presence and chooses which of opposing companions—angel or devil, reason or desire, truth or falsehood, and so forth—to follow, since settled companionship is hard to break. | mentions 9:119
[RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Raising the hands signals leaving both worlds and directing all inner faculties toward God; “God is greatest” means He exceeds all beings, knowledge, comparison, and even the claim that He is simply greater.

[RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Muhammad's ascent has a bodily journey from Mecca to Jerusalem and then the high kingdom, and a spiritual journey from the visible to the unseen and from the unseen to the unseen of the unseen. | mentions 53:9

[BAYDAWI:1:5/r2] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | holds | Arabs vary person and address to refresh speech and engage listeners; Bayḍāwī illustrates the shift with Qur'anic examples and Imruʾ al-Qays's changing pronouns. | mentions 10:22, 35:9
[BAYDAWI:1:5/r20] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | reports | Another analysis takes the conjunction as circumstantial: “We worship You while seeking Your help.”
[BAYDAWI:1:5/r21] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | reports | Kasra on both nūns follows Tamim dialect, which kasras imperfect prefixes other than yāʾ if the following vowel is not ḍamma.
[BAYDAWI:1:5/r3] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | holds | Iyyā is a detached accusative pronoun; attached yāʾ, kāf, or hāʾ marks person and has no syntactic position, like tāʾ in anta and kāf in araʾaytaka.
[BAYDAWI:1:5/r4] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl analyzes iyyā as a noun to which attached pronouns are genitive, citing an Arab saying about a man reaching sixty and young women.
[BAYDAWI:1:5/r5] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | rejects | Bayḍāwī dismisses al-Khalīl's evidence as anomalous and unreliable.
[BAYDAWI:1:5/r6] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | reports | One analysis makes suffixes the pronouns and iyyā their support because pronouns detached from governors cannot be pronounced alone.
[BAYDAWI:1:5/r7] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | reports | Another analysis treats the whole form—iyyā plus suffix—as the pronoun.
[BAYDAWI:1:5/r8] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | reports | Reported readings include iyyāka with fatḥa on hamza and hiyyāka with hamza changed to hāʾ.
[BAYDAWI:1:5/r9] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | holds | ʿIbāda is utmost submission and humility, from maʿbad, a smoothed road, and a garment of exceptional thickness; thus it is used only for submission to God.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:1:5#2/r1] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Necessary aid makes action possible; nonessential aid makes it easier or encourages it, but is not required for moral responsibility.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:1:5#2/r10] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | The imperfect verbs with kasra are a Tamīm dialect feature when the following consonant is not uḍamma.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:1:5#2/r2] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | The request may seek help in all important matters or specifically in performing acts of worship; the pronoun can include the reciter, angels present, congregants, or all monotheists.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:1:5#2/r3] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The speaker includes himself among worshippers to seek acceptance and response through their blessing, which helps explain the institution of congregational prayer.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:1:5#2/r4] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Fronting إياك conveys honor, concern, and exclusivity; Ibn ʿAbbās glosses it “we worship You and worship no other.”
[BAYDAWI-FULL:1:5#2/r5] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The worshipper should attend first to the worshipped and regard worship as a noble relation to God, not as a self-congratulatory act.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:1:5#2/r6] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The Prophet's statement “God is with us” is superior to Moses' “my Lord is with me” because the former loses sight of self in divine presence. | ment

[BAYDAWI-FULL:1:5#2/r7] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Repeating إياك explicitly reserves seeking help for God, while placing worship first preserves rhyme and teaches that presenting a means before one's request aids its acceptance.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:1:5#2/r8] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Saying “we worship” might sound boastful, so “we seek Your help” clarifies that worship itself depends on God's aid and enabling.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:1:5#2/r9] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | The conjunction may instead express circumstance: “we worship You while seeking Your help.”
[BAYDAWI-FULL:1:5/r1] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | After identifying the one worthy of praise, the discourse turns from absence to direct address and from reasoning to witnessing: the servants reserve worship and seeking aid for Him.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:1:5/r2] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The shift of person is an Arabic device that refreshes speech and engages listeners, as in 10:22 and 35:9 and the cited poetry of Imruʾ al-Qays. | mentions 10:22, 35:9
[BAYDAWI-FULL:1:5/r3] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | إيا is the accusative pronoun stem and the attached letters distinguish speaker, addressee, and absent person; the attached forms have no grammatical case of their own.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:1:5/r4] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl considered the following suffix to be annexed to إيا, citing a colloquial example; al-Bayḍāwī says this evidence is anomalous and unreliable.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:1:5/r5] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | Other grammatical analyses treat إيا as the pronoun with an added support element, or treat the entire form as the pronoun.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:1:5/r6] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | Readings include opening إيا's hamza and replacing it with hāʾ.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:1:5/r7] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | ʿIbāda is the utmost submission and abasement, and is used only for submission to God.
[NASAFI:1:1/r12] NASAFI, d. 710 · أبو هريرة عن النبي | reports | Abu Hurayra reports God’s dialogue dividing the Fatiha between Himself and the servant: praise, glorification, and exaltation belong to God; the worshipper’s request for guidance and the response to it belong to the servant, while worship and aid are shared.
[NASAFI:1:5/r1] NASAFI, d. 710 · الخليل وسيبويه | reports | Al-Khalil and Sibawayh parse iyya as an independent pronoun; for Sibawayh the kaf is an uninflected address particle, while for al-Khalil it is an attached pronoun in annexation to iyya.
[NASAFI:1:5/r2] NASAFI, d. 710 · الكوفيون | reports | The Kufans regard iyaka as a complete pronoun rather than dividing it into iyya and the kaf.
[NASAFI:1:5/r3] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | holds | Putting the object before the verb expresses exclusivity: worshippers devote worship, the utmost humility and submission, and their request for aid to God alone.
[NASAFI:1:5/r4] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | holds | The verse shifts from speaking about God in the third person to addressing Him directly after praise establishes His attributes and greatness; the worshipper turns to the uniquely worthy addressee to worship and seek help from no other.
[NASAFI:1:5/r5] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | holds | Iltifat can shift from third person to address, address to third person, or third person to first person; Nasafi illustrates the pattern with shifts in Qur’an 10:22 and 35:9 and Imru’ al-Qays’s poem, where the speaker changes person across its three lines. | mentions 10:22, 35:9
[NASAFI:1:5/r6] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | holds | Arabs favor shifts of style because they engage listeners, renew attention, and make listening more pleasurable; particular placements also carry subtleties recognized by expert scholars.
[NASAFI:1:5/r7] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | reports | Worship precedes asking for aid either because presenting a means before asking for a need makes a response likelier, or to preserve the verse order, as with al-Rahman’s precedence despite the greater rhetorical force of the other name.
[NASAFI:1:5/r8] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | holds | The unqualified request for aid embraces every kind of help; alternatively, it asks God’s help and enabling for worship, with ‘guide us’ specifying the requested assistance. | mentions 1:6
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p7#3/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | reports | Sibawayh treats iya as a detached pronoun and the kaf as an address particle without syntactic position; al-Khalil treats iya as the pronoun with the kaf attached to it.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p7#3/r2] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · الكوفيون | reports | The Kufans treat the whole form iyaka as one pronoun.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p7#3/r3] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Fronting the object marks exclusivity: worship and the seeking of aid are directed to God alone; worship is the utmost submission and abasement.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p7#3/r4] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The shift from third-person reference to direct address is iltifat; Arabic rhetoric uses such shifts to refresh attention and heighten reception, and the cited Qur'anic and poetic examples illustrate its forms. | mentions 10:22, 30:48
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p7#3/r5] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Direct address follows the great descriptions of God: the one worthy of praise, humility, and aid is addressed as the uniquely distinguished Lord described above.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p7#3/r6] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | reports | Worship precedes asking for aid because presenting the means before a request brings a response closer; alternatively, the order follows the preceding arrangement of the verses.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p7#3/r7] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The request for aid is unrestricted and covers every need; alternatively it asks for God's help and enabling grace in performing acts of worship, which the following request for guidance specifies.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r1] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | Iyyā takes attached first, second, or third person pronouns and forms an independent accusative pronoun, not an overt noun with an annexed suffix, contrary to an unnamed claimant.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r10] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | Annexing iyyā to an overt noun is rare, or a poetic necessity; the text gives examples of both.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r11] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | In the familiar warning use, iyyā can contain a nominative pronoun that is followed by a nominative emphatic pronoun.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r12] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · الجمهور | reports | The majority explain worship as humility and submission, which Abū Ḥayyān later identifies as the basic lexical sense.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r13] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · ابن السكيت | reports | Ibn al-Sikkīt gives tajrīd, stripping or devotion, as an alternative meaning of worship.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r14] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | The transitive sense changes with form: ʿabadt al-rajul means I humbled the man, while ʿabadt Allāh means I humbled myself to God.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r15] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · الحسن، وأبو مجلز، وأبو المتوكل | reports | Al-Ḥasan, Abū Majliz, and Abū al-Mutawakkil read iyyāka yaʿbudu with yāʾ and a passive verb.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r16] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · بعض أهل مكة | reports | Some Meccans read naʿbud with the dāl unvowelled.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r17] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · زيد بن علي، ويحيى بن وثاب، وعبيد بن عمير الليثي | reports | Zayd ibn ʿAlī, Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb, and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr al-Laythī read naʿbud with kasra on its initial nūn.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r18] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | Istiʿāna means seeking aid; the form istifʿala has twelve uses, including request, transformation, treating something as something, and several forms of equivalence or substitution.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r19] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · صاحب اللوامح | reports | The author of al-Lawāmiʿ reports a form wayyāka, with hamza changed to wāw, but is unsure whether it came from al-Farrāʾ or Arab usage.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r2] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | reports | Grammarians differ over whether the pronoun is the whole form or only part of it, whether the suffixes are letters or nouns, and whether iyyā is added solely to host pronouns.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r20] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | The change to wāw reflects aversion to hamza; this reverses the alternative tendency to replace a kasra-bearing wāw with hamza.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r21] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · أبو الحسن بن سيده | reports | Ibn Sīda says tamāsaktu, masaktu, amsaktu, and istamsaktu bi-shayʾ have the same sense, holding fast to something; this adds two equivalence uses to istifʿala.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r22] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | Istiʿāna means asking for help, as in other verbs of request.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r23] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · الجمهور | reports | The majority pronounce the initial nūn of nastaʿīn with fatḥa, the Hijazi and most correct form.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r24] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · عبيد بن عمير الليثي، وزر بن حبيش، ويحيى بن وثاب، والنخعي، والأعمش | reports | These readers pronounce the initial nūn of nastaʿīn with kasra, matching Qays, Tamīm, Asad, and Rabīʿa; similar imperfect forms follow the same rule.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r25] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · أبو جعفر الطوسي | reports | Abū Jaʿfar al-Ṭūsī identifies the kasra on the initial nūn as the dialect of Hudhayl.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r26] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | In these forms wāw shifts to alif in istaʿāna and mustaʿān, and to yāʾ in nastaʿīn and mustaʿīn; deletion in istiʿāna belongs to morphology.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r27] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | Istaʿāna can take a direct object or the preposition bi-; its verbal noun also shows morphological deletion.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r28] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | Iyyāka is the fronted direct object of naʿbud.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r29] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · الزمخشري | rejects | Al-Zamakhsharī takes object fronting to mean exclusivity, as though the verse said only you we worship; Abū Ḥayyān says it instead signals care and attention to the object.

YYAN, d. 745 · الجمهور | reports | The majority read iyyā with a kasra on hamza and a doubled yāʾ.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r30] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | An Arab addressed an insulter with iyyāka aʿnī; the reply wa-ʿanka aʿriḍ shows that speakers front what matters most.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r31] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | Iyyāka is an iltifāt from third-person reference, since a consistent third-person construction would say iyyāhu.

[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r33] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | reports | Rhetoricians cite iltifāt as a display of command over expression; some also seek a distinct local effect, and Ibn al-Athīr wrote notably on the device.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r34] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | After praising God for lordship, mercy, and kingship in 1:2–4, the speaker turns to address Him and says that he and others worship and submit to Him. | mentions 1:2, 1:3, 1:4
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r35] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | The first-person plural nūn includes the speaker and others, just as the preceding praise encompasses all who praise.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r36] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | Addressing a present person directly is more tactful and effective than referring to him as absent with iyyāhu.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r37] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | The direct address in iyyāka naʿbud is a preparation for the supplication ihdinā that follows. | mentions 1:6
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r38] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · من ذهب إلى أن ملك منادى | reports | If malik is taken as a vocative, iyyāka continues address rather than making an iltifāt; shifts to third person can nevertheless follow a vocative, as the cited poems show.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r39] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · الزمخشري | rejects | Al-Zamakhsharī counts three iltifāts in Imruʾ al-Qays’s lines, but Abū Ḥayyān identifies only two: address to third person, then third person to first person.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r4] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · الفضل الرقاشي | reports | Al-Faḍl al-Ruqāshī reads it with a fatḥa on hamza and a doubled yāʾ.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r40] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | rejects | Abū Ḥayyān rejects identifying the first shift by inferred presence: iltifāt concerns actual wording, and inserting an unspoken say before either phrase would remove the shift.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r41] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | The passive reading iyyāka yuʿbadu seems to lack a governor for the accusative pronoun; Abū Ḥayyān explains it as a metaphorical substitution of nominative anta, followed by an unusual shift to third person.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r42] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | Worship can also mean obedience, as in the command not to worship Satan. | mentions 19:44
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r43] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | reports | Some interpret worship here as drawing near to God through obedience.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r44] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | reports | Worship is also interpreted as supplication, as in the warning against those who disdain worship. | mentions 40:60
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r45] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | reports | Worship is also explained as affirming God's oneness, as in the statement that jinn and humankind were created only to worship. | mentions 51:56
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r46] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | The meanings offered for worship—humility, obedience, drawing near, supplication, and affirming oneness—are close in sense.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r47] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | Joining worship to seeking help combines what the servant offers God with what the servant asks from Him.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r48] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | Worship precedes the request for aid because the means is presented before the need, so the request may be answered.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r49] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | The unqualified terms worship and seeking help encompass every act of worship and every matter for which help is sought.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r5] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · عمرو بن فائد | reports | ʿAmr ibn Fāʾid, transmitting from Ubayy, reads it with kasra on hamza and an undoubled yāʾ.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r50] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | Repeating iyyāka makes worship and seeking help two independently intended sentences.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r51] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | The repeated iyyāka explicitly identifies God as the one from whom aid is sought; without it, the wording could leave the source unspecified.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r52] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · بعض المنتمين للصلاح | rejects | Some pious interpreters restrict worship to knowledge and seeking help to gnosis, but Abū Ḥayyān says the wording gives no evidence for these restrictions.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r53] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · قالوا | reports | They say naʿbud refutes the determinists while nastaʿīn refutes the Qadarites.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r54] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | Worship is an exalted station, commanded in scripture and used as an honorific for the most excellent creatures, including the Prophet and Jesus. | mentions 15:99, 2:21, 22:77, 17:1, 2:23, 19:30
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r55] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | The verse God gives in 20:14 places worship after exclusive monotheism, because monotheism is the foundation and worship its branch. | mentions 20:14
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r56] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | Directly addressing God as present refutes materialists, atheists, and those who deny a creator.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r6] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · ابن السوار الغنوي | reports | Ibn al-Sawwār al-Ghanawī reads the forms with either a kasra or fatḥa hamza replaced by hāʾ.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r7] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · أبو عبيدة | rejects | Abū ʿUbayda’s derivation of iyyā is weak; Abū Ḥayyān says he was poor at grammar despite mastery of lexicon and Arab history.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r8] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | reports | If iyyā is derived, proposed sources include the word in a poetic line and āya, with the latter analysis making its root consonant yāʾ.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:5/r9] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | rejects | Several competing root and pattern analyses are proposed for iyyā, but Abū Ḥayyān judges them all weak.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p40#2/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Iyyā plus attached suffixes is an independent accusative pronoun, not a visible noun in construct; grammarians disagree about the status of the base and suffixes.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p40#2/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | The pronoun has several reported pronunciations: kasra or fatḥa on the hamza with doubled yāʾ, light yāʾ, or replacement of hamza by hāʾ.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p40#2/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو عبيدة | rejects | Abū ʿUbayda's derivation of iyyā is weak; Abū Ḥayyān says his expertise was languages and Arab history, not grammar.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p40#2/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Proposed derivations from words for refuge or a verse, along with several morphological reconstructions, are all judged weak.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p40#2/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن السكيت | reports | Ibn al-Sikkīt glosses ʿibāda as tajrīd, while the majority gloss it as humility and submission.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p40#2/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الحسن، وأبو مجلز، وأبو المتوكل | reports | Al-Ḥasan, Abū Majlaz, and Abū al-Mutawakkil read iyyāka yaʿbud in the passive voice.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p40#2/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · بعض أهل مكة | reports | Some Meccans read naʿbud with a quiescent dāl.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p40#2/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · زيد بن علي، ويحيى بن وثاب، وعبيد بن عمير الليثي | reports | Zayd ibn ʿAlī, Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb, and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr al-Laythī read naʿbud with a kasra on its nūn.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p40#2/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Istiʿāna means requesting help, and requesting is one of twelve meanings of the verb pattern istifʿāl, alongside the cited related semantic functions.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p42/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو الحسن بن سيده | reports | Ibn Sīda records tamāsaktu, masaktu, and istamsaktu as equivalent expressions for holding onto something.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p42/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The shift draws the worshipper into direct address after praising God as Lord, Merciful, and King, and prepares the ensuing supplication for guidance.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p42/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Including istifʿāl forms that match tafāʿala and tafaʿʿala raises the pattern's possible meanings from twelve to fourteen.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p42/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الجمهور | reports | The majority pronounce the nūn of nastaʿīn with fatḥa; Abū Ḥayyān calls this the eloquent Ḥijāzī form.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p42/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · عبيد بن عمير الليثي، وزر بن حبيش، ويحيى بن وثاب، والنخعي، والأعمش | reports | These readers use kasra on the nūn, a dialect attributed to Qays, Tamīm, Asad, and Rabīʿa; al-Ṭūsī attributes it to Hudhayl.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p42/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Istiʿāna is derived from the root for help, with regular vowel changes across forms, and takes either a direct object or the preposition bāʾ.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p42/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · صاحب اللوامح | reports | The author of al-Lawāmiḥ records a form wayyāka with wāw substituted for hamza, though he is unsure whether it comes from al-Farrāʾ or Arab usage.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p42/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī says fronting iyyāka restricts worship to God alone, equivalent to saying We worship no one but You.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p42/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | Abū Ḥayyān rejects compulsory restriction from fronting: it may express attention and care for the object, as ordinary Arabic examples show.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p42/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Iyyāka is an iltifāt from third-person reference to direct address; iltifāt shifts amo
