[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p43#2/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الجمهور | reports | Most interpret worship as submission and humility; other contextual senses include obedience, drawing near through obedience, supplication, and affirmation of divine unity. | mentions 19:44, 40:60, 51:56
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p43#2/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Worship is joined to seeking help because the verse combines what the servant offers God with what the servant asks from Him; worship comes first as a means before the request.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p43#2/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Both worship and seeking help are unqualified so they include every act of worship and every matter for which help is sought.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p43#2/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Repeating iyyāka makes worship and seeking help two deliberate clauses and explicitly identifies God as the one from whom help is requested.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p43#2/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · بعض المنتمين للصلاح | reports | Some spiritually inclined interpreters assign worship to knowledge and seeking help to mystical gnosis, but Abū Ḥayyān finds no textual indication for these restrictions.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p43#2/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Some say We worship answers the determinists and We seek help answers the advocates of free will.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p43#2/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Worship is a noble station: scripture applies servant to prophets and places worship after monotheism, since worship follows the foundation of divine unity. | mentions 17:1, 2:23, 19:30, 21:25
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p43#2/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Some read the direct address in iyyāka as an answer to deniers of time, God, or a creator, because it addresses a present existent.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p43/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | If malik is a vocative, iyyāka is not a shift from absence, since it continues direct address after direct address.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p43/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | Abū Ḥayyān rejects al-Zamakhsharī's three-iltifāt analysis of Imruʾ al-Qays's lines, finding two shifts and rejecting the proposed movement to presence.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p43/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | The passive reading iyyāka yuʿbadu is grammatically difficult because iyyāka is accusative; Abū Ḥayyān explains it through metaphorical pronoun substitution and an internal shift.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p54/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The sūra uses fronting and delay in “we worship, we seek help” and in “those angered, those astray.”
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p54/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The shift to direct address in “You alone we worship,” “You alone we seek help,” and “guide us” is iltifāt.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p54/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · عمرو بن عبيد | reports | In an anomalous count, ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd treats “You alone we worship” as a verse, giving eight verses.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:5#2/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The present verb is nominative because it has no governing subjunctive or jussive; Basran grammarians also explain this by its occupying a noun's position and resembling nouns in form and distribution.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:5#2/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The subject of naʿbudu is obligatorily implicit.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:5#2/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Worship is ultimate submission, due only to the ultimate benefactor, and is stronger than ʿubūdiyya, which is outwardly showing submission.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:5#2/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The root denotes submission: a trodden road is called muʿabbad, as are a subdued camel and a person made submissive by tar.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:5#2/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · طرفة | reports | Ṭarafa's line uses muʿabbad for a road, illustrating the sense of a road trodden smooth.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:5#2/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The phrase shifts from speaking about God in the third person to addressing Him directly, a rhetorical turn; Yūnus 10:22 offers the reverse direction. | mentions 10:22
[SAMIN-DURR:1:5#2/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · بعضهم | rejects | Some critics correct al-Zamakhsharī's count to two shifts, rather than three; the author answers that the opening address itself shifts from the expected first person.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:5#2/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The Imruʾ al-Qays example has three shifts: first person to address, then to third person, then back to first person.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:5#3/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | A rare reading has a third-person passive form, analyzed as borrowing an accusative pronoun for a nominative subject, with the underlying sense أنت تعبد.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:5#3/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The anomalous form also shifts from direct address in إياك to third person in يعبد; the author calls this an unusual shift within one clause.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:5#3/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الآخر | reports | A poet uses the second-person suffix in عصيكا where the expected first-person form would be عصيت, illustrating a pronoun substitution parallel.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:5#3/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | A fronted object pronoun is obligatory when a delayed object would have to attach to its verb; this rule does not apply when attachment is optional.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:5#3/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The syntax of إياك نستعين parallels إياك نعبد, and the conjunction coordinates both inflection and meaning.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:5#3/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الجمهور | reports | Most grammarians say the conjunction does not establish sequence; a group of Kufans disagrees.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:5#3/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Nastaʿīnu derives from nastaʿwinu: a preceding kasra changes the quiescent wāw to yāʾ, as in mīzān and mīqāt.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:5#3/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The sīn marks requesting help, while استفعل also conveys adoption, transformation, finding or deeming, causative and related meanings, and sometimes replaces other verb patterns.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:5#4/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | A dialect reads the imperfect prefix with kasra under stated conditions: not before yāʾ, and with a past stem having medial kasra, initial hamzat al-waṣl, or a reflexive tāʾ; ordinary forms such as yaḍribu lack these conditions.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:5#4/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | The supposed restriction against yāʾ is challenged by the reported form ييلمون, while ييجل is offered as an attempted sound-easing exception. | mentions 4:104
[SAMIN-DURR:1:5#4/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · النابغة الجعدي | reports | Al-Nābigha asks Laylā al-Akhyaliyya whether they take shelter from severe cold; her kasra-prefix reply نكتني prompts his bawdy joke and demonstrates the dialect.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:5#4/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Seeking help is requesting assistance and support.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:5#4/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Worship precedes the request for help because worship is the means leading to a requested need.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:5#4/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Neither verb names an object, allowing the wording to encompass every object of worship or aid, or to focus on performing the acts without regard to an object.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:5#4/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The objectless wording can also present eating and drinking simply as acts to perform. | mentions 2:60
[SAMIN-DURR:1:5/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Iyyaka is the object placed before na'budu for exclusivity and must be a detached form.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:5/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Most grammarians classify iyyaka as a pronoun, while al-Zajjaj treats it as an overt noun.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:5/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Pronoun analyses differ: the whole form is a pronoun; only iyya is; iyya plus suffix marker is; or iyya is support and the suffix is the pronoun.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:5/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | The rare phrase iyaha al-shawab annexes iyya to an overt noun, supporting the analysis that suffixes are genitive annexes.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:5/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | Some derive iyyā from aw or āya and debate its pattern, but the author says this is useless because morphology does not apply to deeply frozen forms.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:5/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The common form has kasra and doubled y; other forms open the hamza or replace it with hā', with doubled or plain y, as a poem shows.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:5/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Some reject the light pronunciation because it could sound like we worship your sun; the text notes irregular readings among the variants without detailing them.
[IBNKATHIR:1:5/r1] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · القراء السبعة والجمهور | reports | The seven readers and the majority pronounce the yāʾ in iyyāka with gemination.
[IBNKATHIR:1:5/r10] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The opening is God's praise of Himself and instruction to servants to praise Him; the Prophet says prayer is invalid without reciting the Opening of the Book when able.
[IBNKATHIR:1:5/r11] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · الله تعالى | reports | In a divine report, God divides the prayer between Himself and His servant, responds to each recited section, calls 1:5 shared between them, and grants the servant's request.
[IBNKATHIR:1:5/r12] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says the servant worships, fears, and hopes in God alone, and seeks His help for obedience and every affair.
[IBNKATHIR:1:5/r13] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · قتادة | reports | Qatadah says God commands His servants to devote worship sincerely to Him and seek His help for their affairs.
[IBNKATHIR:1:5/r14] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | Worship precedes asking for help because worship is the intended end

 while seeking help is its means; sound judgment puts the more important matter first.
[IBNKATHIR:1:5/r15] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | reports | One explanation of the plural nūn is that the speaker represents the whole class of worshippers, including fellow believers, especially in congregational prayer or when leading them.
[IBNKATHIR:1:5/r16] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · بعضهم | reports | Another explanation allows a plural of honor: the servant is noble while worshipping, but should not claim collective standing outside worship because everyone depends on God.
[IBNKATHIR:1:5/r17] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · بعضهم | reports | A third view says we is more humble than I worship because the singular could imply that one person alone can fully worship or properly praise God.
[IBNKATHIR:1:5/r18] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | Servanthood is an exalted station; God calls His Messenger His servant at the revelation, public worship, and night journey, and directs him to worship amid rejection. | mentions 18:1, 72:19, 17:1, 15:97, 15:98, 15:99
[IBNKATHIR:1:5/r19] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · بعضهم | reports | Some argue that servanthood is nobler than messengerhood because worship proceeds from creation to God, while the messenger's mission proceeds from God to creation; Ibn Kathir rejects the claim and its reasoning.
[IBNKATHIR:1:5/r2] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · عمرو بن فايد | reports | Amr ibn Fayd's light yāʾ with kasra is a rejected anomalous reading because iyā means sunlight.
[IBNKATHIR:1:5/r20] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · بعض الصوفية | reports | Some Sufis criticize worship motivated by reward or avoidance of punishment, and even worship as honor through religious duties, arguing that the highest worship is for God's own perfection.
[IBNKATHIR:1:5/r21] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · آخرون | rejects | Others rebut the Sufi criticism: worship directed to God can still seek reward and protection from punishment, as the Prophet affirms to a Bedouin asking for Paradise and refuge from Hell.
[IBNKATHIR:1:5/r3] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · بعض القراء | reports | Some read ayyaka with an open hamza and geminated yāʾ, while others substitute hāʾ for hamza, as illustrated by a poetic line.
[IBNKATHIR:1:5/r4] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · يحيى بن وثاب والأعمش | reports | All readers open the initial nūn of nastaʿīn except Yahya ibn Waththab and al-A'mash, who use kasra, a dialect of several Arab tribes.
[IBNKATHIR:1:5/r5] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | In ordinary language ʿibādah is rooted in humility, as in a subdued road or camel; in religious usage it combines complete love, submission, and fear.
[IBNKATHIR:1:5/r6] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | Fronting and repeating iyyāka marks special concern and restriction: worship is for God alone and reliance is on Him alone, the perfection of obedience.
[IBNKATHIR:1:5/r7] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · بعض السلف | reports | Some early authorities call this the secret of the Fatiha, itself the secret of the Qur'an: the first clause renounces shirk and the second renounces self-power through surrender to God.
[IBNKATHIR:1:5/r8] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | Worship and reliance recur together elsewhere in the Qur'an, including commands to worship God and trust Him. | mentions 11:123, 67:29, 73:9
[IBNKATHIR:1:5/r9] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | The speech shifts from speaking of God in the third person to addressing Him directly because praise brings the worshipper near and present before Him.
[BURHAN:v1p16/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · القاضي أبو بكر بن العربي | reports | Ibn al-ʿArabī estimates the Qurʾānic sciences at fifty categories and a further vast total calculated by multiplying the Qurʾān’s words by four.
[BURHAN:v1p16/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · بعض السلف | reports | Some early authorities say each Qurʾānic word has an outward sense, an inward sense, a limit, and a point of departure; relations among words exceed human enumeration.
[BURHAN:v1p16/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · القاضي أبو بكر بن العربي | reports | Ibn al-ʿArabī groups the Qurʾān’s core subjects into monotheism, reminder—including promise, warning, Paradise, Hell, and purification—and rulings, including duties and commands.
[BURHAN:v1p16/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Al-Fātiḥa is the Mother of the Book because it contains all three fields: monotheism through 1:4, rulings in 1:5, and reminder from 1:6 onward.
[BURHAN:v1p16/r5] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | reports | The claim that Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ equals a third of the Qurʾān is explained either as a reward granted by God or as a meaning-based division, since it contains monotheism. | mentions 112:1
[BURHAN:v1p16/r6] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | reports | One explanation for the title “Mother of the Book” is that al-Fātiḥa precedes the rest of the Qurʾān as a mother precedes a daughter.
[BURHAN:v1p16/r7] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | reports | Another explanation of “Opening” is that al-Fātiḥa opens the gates of Paradise, as discussed elsewhere.
[BURHAN:v1p16/r8] BURHAN, d. 794 · أبو الحكم بن برجان | reports | Ibn Barrajān divides Qurʾānic knowledge into God’s names and attributes, prophethood and its proofs, and legal obligation and trial; the last is hardest because it is unfamiliar and neglected.
[BURHAN:v1p260#2/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · بعض الأئمة | reports | Some imams say al-Fatiha affirms lordship, seeks guidance in Islam, and asks protection from Judaism and Christianity.
[BURHAN:v1p359/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | rejects | The author says the familiar labels for stop quality are not a complete, sound classification and have produced confusion in books on pauses.
[BURHAN:v1p359/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | A forced pause is caused only by running out of breath and is not restricted to particular places; examples include Ḥamza pausing within words or before a genitive complement. | mentions 2:207
[BURHAN:v1p359/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | prefers | An optional pause is preferable and is classified by how the two parts of the statement depend on each other.
[BURHAN:v1p359/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | A complete pause leaves both adjoining parts independently sufficient; stopping at “we ask for help” is complete because the following request also stands alone. | mentions 1:6
[BURHAN:v1p436/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | These insights benefit only someone sincere, reflective, and shaped by the Qurʾān in heart and action; otherwise conduct contradicts professed words.
[BURHAN:v1p436/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | reports | A spiritual adept feared that relying on another person after praying “You alone we ask for help” would make his prayer a lie; likewise, following Satan’s counsel contradicts seeking refuge from him.
[BURHAN:v1p63/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | reports | One explanation for putting the request for help after worship, though help precedes worship in sense, is that the order suits the sūrah’s verse endings.
[BURHAN:v2p320/r7] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The supplicatory meaning of “we ask for help” is “help us in Your worship.”
[BURHAN:v3p10/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | reports | One explanation for repeating “You alone” is emphasis, like repeating “between” in “between Zayd and between ʿAmr.”
[BURHAN:v3p10/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | reports | Another explanation is that omission would attach a following pronoun to the second verb and lose the intended emphasis created by placing its object first.
[BURHAN:v3p10/r5] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | rejects | The author says no explanation for the repeated object is needed: two different verbs each require an object, so stating both is normal and deletion would be exceptional.
[BURHAN:v3p235/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · سيبويه | reports | Sībawayh says that when coordinated matters are both important, Arabic speakers put first the one that matters more or deserves greater attention; the conjunction itself does not order them.
[BURHAN:v3p235/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Worship precedes the request for help because worship is the more important matter.
[BURHAN:v3p235/r7] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Fronting the object in “You alone we worship” expresses exclusive worship: we worship You and no one else.
[BURHAN:v3p247/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Worship comes before seeking aid because it is the cause of receiving aid.
[BURHAN:v3p322/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Al-Fātiḥa begins in third-person style through “Master of the Day of Judgment,” then turns to direct address with “You alone we worship.” | mentions 1:4
[BURHAN:v3p325/r5] BURHAN, d. 794 · البيانيون | reports | Rhetoricians say changing a style after a long stretch refreshes the listener, draws attention, broadens expression, and eases meter and rhyme.
[BURHAN:v3p325/r6] BURHAN, d. 794 · القاضي شمس الدين بن الجوزي | reports | Ibn al-Jawzī argues that stylistic variation alone does not explain appropriateness, since a long Qurʾānic list in 33:35 maintains one style throughout. | mentions 33:35
[BURHAN:v3p325/r7] BURHAN, d. 794 · القاضي شمس الدين بن الجوزي | reports | Ibn al-Jawzī explains the shift from praise to direct address by the listener’s changing attention: the praise awakens the heart, making “You alone” apt.
[BURHAN:v3p325/r8] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The particular reasons for a shift of style depend on its setting and on the speaker’s purpose.
[BURHAN:v3p326/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The successive praises intensify the servant's attention: God's exclusive praise, universal lordship, gifts of mercy, and command of judgment prepare the worshipper to approach and seek help.
[BURHAN:v3p326/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · قيل | reports | One explanation says praise uses third person because it ranks below worship, while direct address elevates the worshipper's encounter; similarly, blessing is explicitly attributed to God but anger is phrased obliquely as a matter of etiquette. | mentions 6:101
[BURHAN:v3p326/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · قيل | reports | Another explanation says that after describing God with magnificent attributes, the discours

[BURHAN:v3p327/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Human beings begin distant from God behind the veil of majesty; knowing and praising Him and worshipping as befits them makes them ready to address Him directly.
[BURHAN:v3p327/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Before prayer and intimate address, worshippers should present God’s attributes with reverence, rather than pray carelessly, playfully, or without intention.
[BURHAN:v3p327/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Intimate prayer rises only after purification from ignorance of God, analogously to bodily prayer after ritual purification; this explains placing refuge-seeking before recitation.
[NASHR:v1p226/r1] NASHR, d. 833 · author | holds | A complete stop commonly comes at verse ends and story endings; he illustrates one at māliki yawm al-dīn, followed by the start iyyāka naʿbudu.
[NASHR:v1p227/r1] NASHR, d. 833 · author | holds | Both māliki yawm al-dīn and iyyāka naʿbudu permit a complete stop, but the first is more complete because the second shares the address's meaning with what follows.
[NASHR:v1p47/r1] NASHR, d. 833 · author | rejects | He rejects the claim that the seven ahruf mean following seven famous imams; readings must be received reliably, word by word, through successive imams to the Prophet.
[NASHR:v1p47/r12] NASHR, d. 833 · author | holds | Maki deems these noncanonical-imam readings permissible when reliably transmitted, since each has a sound Arabic analysis and agrees with the codex spelling; Ibn al-Jazari says others also share some forms.
[NASHR:v1p47/r8] NASHR, d. 833 · عمرو بن فائد الإسواري | reports | Amr b. Fa'id reads both instances of iyyāka with a light yā'; some later scholars disliked it because it sounds like iyā, the sun's light.
[NASHR:v1p47/r9] NASHR, d. 833 · يحيى بن وثاب | reports | Yahya b. Waththab reads the first nūn of nastaʿīn with kasra, a well-known and good dialect.
[NASHR:v1p48/r11] NASHR, d. 833 · الفضل بن محمد الرقاشي | reports | Al-Fadl b. Muhammad al-Raqashi reads both instances with fatḥa on the hamza; the source also transmits it from Ali through Sufyan al-Thawri.
[NASHR:v1p48/r12] NASHR, d. 833 · أبو عمرو | reports | Abu Amr, through Abd Allah b. Dawud al-Khuraybi, reads the alif of both instances of iyyāka with imāla because of the preceding kasra.
[NASHR:v1p48/r13] NASHR, d. 833 · بعض أهل مكة | reports | Some Meccans read naʿbud with a still dāl for lightening, or treat it as a verse ending and carry a pause into connected recitation.
[NASHR:v1p49/r7] NASHR, d. 833 · قتيبة عن الكسائي، كردم عن نافع، ورش | reports | The author adds unlisted transmissions: Qutayba from al-Kisa'i has imāla in al-ʿālamīn and al-raḥmān; Kurram from Nafi and al-Ahwazi from Warsh lengthen vowels in mālik, naʿbudu, and iyyāka.
[BIQAI:1:5/r1] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | After God's entitlement and mercy have been established, a rational person turns to Him alone; the passage shifts from speaking about Him to addressing Him directly.
[BIQAI:1:5/r10] BIQAI, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Al-Ḥarālī says all Qur'an is God's speech: some speaks about God Himself, while other passages express what people at varying levels and in varying states ought to say.
[BIQAI:1:5/r11] BIQAI, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Because creatures cannot reach the full truth of what they owe, God, the trustee over all things, informs them of it and makes their recitation equivalent to their own utterance, completing His grace to them.
[BIQAI:1:5/r12] BIQAI, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Left to themselves, people could not say what would mend their worldly and religious condition or adequately thank God; He teaches them words that fulfill their duty, so their sole connection is reciting His sublime speech, with or without understanding.
[BIQAI:1:5/r13] BIQAI, d. 885 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Al-Ḥarālī cites the authenticated report in which the Prophet conveys God's statement that prayer is divided equally between God and His servant, then recites this sūra.
[BIQAI:1:5/r14] BIQAI, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Al-Ḥarālī says the first three verses praise God Himself; when the servant recites them, God accepts that recitation as the servant's praise, eulogy, and glorification.
[BIQAI:1:5/r15] BIQAI, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | For al-Ḥarālī, the following verses are voiced on the creatures' tongues: worship is the servant's duty, while asking for aid belongs to God; the passage is shared between them.
[BIQAI:1:5/r16] BIQAI, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | God's side comes first because His assistance precedes worship and makes it possible.
[BIQAI:1:5/r17] BIQAI, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Al-Ḥarālī says whoever seeks God's aid for a burden according to this verse receives help proportionate to it; failure comes from forfeiting one's share of God, ignorance of the verse's implications, or heedlessness of its blessing.
[BIQAI:1:5/r18] BIQAI, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | The first-person plural nūn in naʿbudu signals that prayer is founded on congregational worship.
[BIQAI:1:5/r19] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | The verse teaches believers to acknowledge incapacity, feel their need, and rely on God's power; this directs their desires toward asking Him for guidance on the straight path. | mentions 1:6
[BIQAI:1:5/r2] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | The direct address names the possessor of the preceding attributes; putting the means of worship before the requested need is more likely to bring a response.
[BIQAI:1:5/r3] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | The phrase guides people toward worshipping God.
[BIQAI:1:5/r4] BIQAI, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Al-Ḥarālī defines worship as reaching the utmost degree in all forms of humble submission.
[BIQAI:1:5/r5] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | Repeating the object pronoun urges earnestness in asking for help; the wording also declares that worship is possible only through God's aid and that guidance rests in His hand.
[BIQAI:1:5/r6] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | The sūra begins with God's essence, points to His acts, rises to His attributes, and returns to His essence, signaling that He encompasses beginning and end.
[BIQAI:1:5/r7] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | Knowledge of God's acts and attributes establishes His right to exclusive worship and then reveals the worshipper's inability to fulfill that right, prompting the request for aid.

[BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r2] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · أبو الفضل محمد المشدالي المغربي | reports | Al-Mashdali's method for Qur'anic coherence is to identify a surah's purpose, its prerequisites and their distance from the goal, then answer expectations raised as the discourse unfolds.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | A surah's name summarizes its purpose, as a title signals the details within; Adam demonstrated this naming principle when he named things before the angels.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r4] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The Fatiha's many titles converge on مراقبة: it is the Mother of the Book, foundation, oft-repeated, treasure, healing, sufficing, complete, protecting, incantation, praise, thanks, supplication and prayer.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r5] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The Fatiha is a treasure, cure, sufficiency, fulfillment, protection and incantation; it gathers praise, gratitude and supplication, with prayer as their greatest assembly.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p12/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The Fatiha's purpose is to establish God's exclusive right to all praise and perfection, sovereignty over both worlds, worship and aid, and to ask for the path of the successful rather than the doomed; its center is مراقبة.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p12/r2] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Prophets, scriptures and laws ultimately gather people to truth so they may know their sovereign and what pleases Him; knowledge and practice together serve the Qur'an's purpose.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r2] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | The basmala relates to the Fatiha as the Fatiha relates to the Qur'an: each is a compact synthesis of what the larger whole details.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p16/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | After establishing God's worthiness and prompting hope and fear, the recitation turns from third person to direct address and puts the means before the request.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p16/r2] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Iyyaka addresses the possessor of these attributes, and worship means reaching the utmost abasement; repeating the pronoun intensifies the request for aid.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p16/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Worship is possible only through God's aid, and guidance lies in His hand; the sequence moves from essence to acts to attributes and back to essence, teaching dependence after recognizing God's right.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p16/r4] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · عائشة | reports | Aisha reports the Prophet seeking refuge in God's pardon from punishment, pleasure from anger, and God from God, then admitting he cannot enumerate His praise.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p16/r5] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Al-Harali says all Qur'an is God's speech, but some verses voice what creatures at different levels ought to say yet cannot express; God teaches

[BIQAI-FULL:v1p16/r6] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Al-Harali explains the sound report that God divided prayer between Himself and His servant: the first three verses are God's praise, which He accepts from the reciting servant as praise and glorification.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p16/r7] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Al-Harali says the paired verse belongs between God and servant: worship is the servant's commitment, aid is God's gift, and aid precedes and enables worship.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p16/r8] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Whoever asks God for aid with a genuine task receives help proportionate to it; failure comes from neglecting God's due, misunderstanding the verse or forgetting its favor, and the plural nun signals congregational prayer.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p16/r9] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The verse teaches confession of inability, need and reliance on God's power; that dependence leads directly to asking for guidance along the necessary path.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p18#2/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The Qur'an's arrangement is miraculous, so the Fatiha must retain its required order in prayer; rearrangement or insertion of foreign material invalidates it. Al-Isfahani locates its clearest inimitability in order.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p18#2/r4] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The spiritual seeker passes through awe of God's attributes, recognizes many perilous paths and the lack of guidance or safety apart from God, then asks for the straight path, its blessed companions and protection from both condemned groups.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p18#2/r5] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · مسعود التفتازاني | reports | Al-Taftazani maps the Fatiha's blessings to two creations and two preservations: creation in Rabb al-alamin, preservation in mercy, second creation in judgment, and afterlife preservation in worship onward.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p18#2/r7] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Al-Harali says the seven repeated verses are the Qur'an's gathered essence and its contents will be disclosed at creation's completion; earlier scriptures progress from changeable scrolls and lasting books to the Qur'an, which completes religion. | mentions 5:3
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Al-Harali contrasts the Qur'an's detailed, dispersed sequence with the Fatiha's seven complete universals, and makes the Fatiha a mirror of the servant's move from misguidance to guidance. | mentions 93:7
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r2] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A Prophetic report says he was sent to complete noble character; the author links this completion with the Fatiha's comprehensive opening and the Qur'an's culmination. | mentions 5:3
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Al-Harali describes the Qur'an's majesty through rulings spanning immediate and deferred realities, witnessed experience, and reports of the past and patterns that recur in time.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r4] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Al-Harali distinguishes gradual descent that moves understanding between states and rulings from descent from high to low, which may occur with or without intermediaries.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r5] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The passage names al-Baqara 2:281 as the last revealed verse and says its recitation position between the debt verse and the verse before it shows revelation and recitation order can differ. | mentions 2:281, 75:17
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Al-Harali says the Qur'an's sevenfold gathering in Muhammad's heart relates to the Mother of Qur'an's universals as the Qur'an's gathering in his heart relates to the Mother.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r2] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Al-Harali says the Qur'an reached the Prophet on his tongue over the span of the prophetic mission, after its descent to the lowest heaven.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · عائشة | reports | Aisha reports that Muhammad's character was the Qur'an, making his conduct the visible form of its inner reality.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r4] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Al-Harali says the Fatiha is the Qur'an's mother: its first three verses encompass the divine names and attributes, while its last three cover the creature's way to God, mercy or failure. | mentions 2:281, 75:17, 33:50, 33:52
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r5] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Recitation order can differ from revelation chronology; the verse allowing the Prophet to marry certain women was placed before a later restriction. | mentions 33:50, 33:52
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r6] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · أبو هريرة | reports | In the authentic report in Muslim and the four Sunan, God says the Fatiha is divided between Himself and His servant: He answers praise, glorification and worship, and grants the servant's final requests.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Al-Baqara aims to prove the Book is guidance to follow; belief in the unseen, especially resurrection and the afterlife, is its greatest guidance and organizing theme.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r2] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The cow story makes the surah's title apt because resurrection occurs through an apparently slight human cause; it is a clearer sign of divine power than Abraham's story or earlier Israelite resurrections.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The following comparison of hearts and stones shows the guided and astray: hearts become hard and wretched, while stones display fear and yield benefit that reaches God's servants.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r4] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The Book functions like a caliph from the resolute messengers, guiding every matter to the right exit: rejecting it fails, hesitation nearly perishes, and accepting it brings piety and excellence.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r5] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Al-Baqara is also called the Radiant and the Hump: it illuminates guidance and sufficiency, brightens believers' faces at judgment, and exalts belief in the afterlife above every other good after monotheism.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p28#s002/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Al-Harali maps al-Fatiha's verses to the seven letters: praise, lawful and forbidden, command and prohibition, clear and ambiguous, then the corresponding petitions; its opening gathers all seven.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p28/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Because praise is the seventh inclusive letter, the Fatiha begins with it and gathers the seven universals diffused through the Qur'an, as the Qur'an gathers earlier scriptures.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p28/r5] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | The fourth verse contains the clear letter in worship and the ambiguous letter in seeking help; because it is intimate direct address, its request is not repeated.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p28/r6] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | The fifth verse's request returns to praise, the sixth to the grace of lawful and forbidden provisions, and the seventh to the sovereign's command; together these complete all seven letters.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p31/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Baqara answers the Fatiha's plea for guidance by directing worshippers to the Book, describing the guided and denied groups as patterns to follow or avoid; its pious are the straight path and its others the path of ruin.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p31/r4] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Alternatively, the surah's purpose is solely to describe the Book; it establishes the truth of its meaning, exposes disbelief and hypocrisy to show that inward faith matters, then proves its inimitable form and authority for teaching law. | mentions 2:21

[ELMALILI:1:5#2/r14] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Hope and fear must be positive and negative effects of one source so the heart can replace one with the other and find contentment; if they come from unrelated sources, pursuit yields endless exhaustion.
[ELMALILI:1:5#2/r15] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The water and fire analogy shows that alternating between hope and fear from unrelated sources is futile; the one Lord is what binds self, consciousness, and the external world.
[ELMALILI:1:5#2/r16] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Worship is obedient action born from the collision of supreme love and fear, seeking ascent from total helplessness to absolute power and seeking tranquility through ultimate humility and reverence.
[ELMALILI:1:5#2/r17] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | True worship unites outward and inward submission without pride or ostentation; arrogant people, heedless optimists, and despairing pessimists are excluded from its honor.
[ELMALILI:1:5#2/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The soul's attachment to an ultimate source of hope and fear is the origin of the innate ideas of worship and the object of worship, and moral character and future fortune depend on its seriousness.
[ELMALILI:1:5#2/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | A person may become wholly captive to one limited pleasure or fear, treating its finite cause as the goal of all love or the limit of all fear and humbling themselves before it.
[ELMALILI:1:5#2/r4] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Such attachment to a created finite cause is the source of shirk and the many false idols, whether animate or inanimate.
[ELMALILI:1:5#2/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Even those who claim no concern with worship continually replace one object of worship with another and live in uncertainty without considering death.
[ELMALILI:1:5#2/r6] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Any heart tied wholly to mortal things is at risk of ruin because that attachment will eventually break; only the Ever-Living Sustainer can guarantee what creatures cannot.
[ELMALILI:1:5#2/r7] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Worship belongs to God alone; worshippers who serve Him are not wholly captured by other hopes and fears and can remain steady in their duties.
[ELMALILI:1:5#2/r8] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · Aleyhi’s-salâtü ve’s-selâm Efendimiz | reports | The Prophet compares a believer to fresh grain that bends in wind and rises again, but a disbeliever to a pine that breaks once and never rises.
[ELMALILI:1:5#2/r9] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The believer is attached to the Everlasting Living God, while the disbeliever is attached to what perishes.
[ELMALILI:1:5#3/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · e‘âzım-ı müfessirîn | reports | The great exegetes paraphrase worship as bowing and humbling oneself only to God, finding tranquility through obedience because He alone is the source of all fear and hope.
[ELMALILI:1:5#3/r10] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The pledge is a heavy burden, but the dignity of God's exaltation is no light goal; human beings cannot undertake it through th

[ELMALILI:1:5#3/r11] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Isti‘ana means asking for aid or assistance; giving help is i‘ana, and mutual assistance is ta‘awun, so the terms must be distinguished.
[ELMALILI:1:5#3/r12] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The exclusive restriction here concerns asking for help; the omitted complement permits three readings: aid itself, aid in every matter, or aid in a specific matter.
[ELMALILI:1:5#3/r13] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The first and universal readings converge in meaning, though the first is more eloquent and the second more explicit.
[ELMALILI:1:5#3/r14] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | rejects | Although worship could suggest a specific request for aid, the verse's monotheistic emphasis and context of God's exclusive praise require a general meaning.
[ELMALILI:1:5#3/r15] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · İbn Abbas | reports | Ibn Abbas's transmitted view supports the general scope of seeking aid, in worship and all other affairs.
[ELMALILI:1:5#3/r16] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The resulting meaning is that believers ask God alone for help both in worship and every other matter, unlike disbelievers who seek help elsewhere.
[ELMALILI:1:5#3/r17] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · Beyzâvî | reports | Beydawi distinguishes necessary aid, without which an act cannot occur, from nonessential aid that makes it easier; necessary aid includes ability, conception, instruments, and material.
[ELMALILI:1:5#3/r18] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Legal theory calls these two kinds of aid enabling power and facilitating power.
[ELMALILI:1:5#3/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | God alone controls fear, hope, pleasure, pain, body, soul, and the inner capacities of perception and volition; these gifts should be devoted to His command with gratitude.
[ELMALILI:1:5#3/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | The proud objector asks whether worship's humility is degrading for a soul that wants to rise or believes it has already risen.
[ELMALILI:1:5#3/r4] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | rejects | Wanting to rise admits one's own need and the value of a higher state, which worship recognizes most fully.
[ELMALILI:1:5#3/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | rejects | Claiming to have risen already falsely treats progress as finite and decline as impossible; ascent is limitless and the danger of falling remains, so worship is pride's remedy.
[ELMALILI:1:5#3/r6] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Humility and reverence toward God provide the highest possible elevation for the human conscience through affiliation with Him.
[ELMALILI:1:5#3/r7] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The imagined worshipper pledges freedom from all but God, obedience to His commands, moral effort, and even sacrifice of life and worlds in God's path.
[ELMALILI:1:5#3/r8] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Such faithful affiliation is the greatest human power and nobility; the Fatiha asks the speaker to say 'we,' making the pledge communal.
[ELMALILI:1:5#3/r9] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The first Muslims lived this spirit and spread God's exaltation across the world, whereas those who lost it bowed to worldly power.
[ELMALILI:1:5#4/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | All enabling aid belongs to God, but the request is ours; capability arises when human seeking and divine assistance coincide with the act, which is called acquisition or partial will.
[ELMALILI:1:5#4/r10] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The limits of understanding human willing reflect our inability to comprehend God's reality.
[ELMALILI:1:5#4/r11] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The verse itself assigns the capacity to seek to us and assistance and power to God, excluding both Jabriyya compulsion and Qadariyya denial of destiny.
[ELMALILI:1:5#4/r12] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | rejects | It is mistaken to infer that every partial will succeeds; when people fail, they may wrongly swing toward compulsion by treating willing as creation and assuming God cannot intervene.
[ELMALILI:1:5#4/r13] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | God can create outcomes that match or diverge from our seeking, grant extra favor to those on His path, or let others face loss, punishment, or reminders.
[ELMALILI:1:5#4/r14] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The verse about entrusting one's affair to God illustrates this subtlety concerning delegated trust. | mentions 40:44
[ELMALILI:1:5#4/r15] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | A hadith says that when God wills to enact His decree, He removes the reason of people of understanding; this concerns good or bad seeking, not compulsion.
[ELMALILI:1:5#4/r16] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The verse says people may dislike what is good for them and love what is harmful, since God knows while they do not. | mentions 2:216
[ELMALILI:1:5#4/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Humans are given authority to request; intended and unintended acts alike are attributed to us because they occur in and through us as their locus.
[ELMALILI:1:5#4/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | In voluntary acts we are the proximate cause through our request, but not the complete cause, since we depend on necessary aid; the Creator makes the total causal set.
[ELMALILI:1:5#4/r4] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Voluntary action expresses a relation between a requesting agent and a creating agent; bodies are inherently passive, while the soul is inherently desirous and God's action is creative.
[ELMALILI:1:5#4/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The engine analogy distinguishes the machine as the locus of motion, the operator as the one who wants and initiates it, and God as the creator of the motion from nonexistence.
[ELMALILI:1:5#4/r6] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | rejects | The account rejects both Jabriyya or materialist views that reduce people to soulless machines and the idea that humans create like God.
[ELMALILI:1:5#4/r7] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Overindulging in metaphysical speculation until one loses the path and denies obvious truths leads to endless error.
[ELMALILI:1:5#4/r8] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The request of existence is not existence itself: seeking is a relation among existents, not a created existent, so it entails neither infinite regress nor compulsion nor creation.
[ELMALILI:1:5#4/r9] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Universal will is created, while partial will, seeking, and choice called kasb are an uncreated relation belonging to us.
[ELMALILI:1:5#5/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The two declarative clauses also perform an implied act of commitment, like conventional oaths, covenants, or contracts; the prior speech signaled the obligation this acceptance entails.
[ELMALILI:1:5#5/r10] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | The author connects this reciprocal moral pattern to the Prophetic hadith, 'Adopt the character traits of God.'
[ELMALILI:1:5#5/r11] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The plural 'we worship / we ask help' gives social community special importance, since the pledge is not expressed in the singular.
[ELMALILI:1:5#5/r12] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · müfessirîn | reports | Exegetes see an indication here of the virtue of congregational worship.
[ELMALILI:1:5#5/r13] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | A congregation is not a mere crowd but an organized body able to act with one spirit, formed through a shared social covenant, so there is no true circularity in the verse.
[ELMALILI:1:5#5/r14] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Social spirit first takes root in individuals when fraternity widens conscience beyond pride, narrowness, and selfishness; this breadth can support anything from a family to an empire.
[ELMALILI:1:5#5/r15] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Narrowness of conscience accompanies ignorance and pride, while an expanded conscience accompanies elevated understanding, humility, mercy, patience, and forbearance; the narrow-hearted person loves and fears only himself.
[ELMALILI:1:5#5/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The verse records a profound covenant between God and servants, a mutual legal agreement that summarizes a fundamental practical and social law of nature.
[ELMALILI:1:5#5/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | All living beings are carried by this covenantal law; disbelievers follow it unconsciously, while believers experience it consciously as well as bodily.
[ELMALILI:1:5#5/r4] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | At the center of the Fatiha, speech and the covenant are voiced through the collective conscience and worshipful tongue, pointing to conscience as a locus for divine speech.
[ELMALILI:1:5#5/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The author links this point to the trustworthy Spirit bringing revelation to Muhammad's heart and to God's speaking to humans by revelation or from behind a veil. | mentions 26:193, 26:194, 42:51
[ELMALILI:1:5#5/r6] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Human speech and communication are gifts from the Creator, so people should hear, understand, and apply God's revealed eternal speech through their shared conscience.
[ELMALILI:1:5#5/r7] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | God models gracious reciprocal dealing: after creating and nurturing people, He gives worldly gifts as if their property and makes them eternal, granting them a nearly equal standing in the agreement.
[ELMALILI:1:5#5/r8] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Although humans have no inherent rights before God, He recognizes their rights and assumes them under His mercy; worship is His right and the servant's duty, while aid, reward, and punishment become human claims by His own commitment.
[ELMALILI:1:5#5/r9] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Rights of people receive even greater care than God's rights; mercy precedes worship, worship precedes asking for help, and duty precedes the claim to a right, though divine mercy establishes the right fi

[ELMALILI:1:5#6/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | When a person shares another’s welfare and harm as their own, social feeling and brotherhood begin; practiced empathy strengthens community and reduces pride.
[ELMALILI:1:5#6/r10] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | As like-minded individuals meet, an actual congregation forms readily and follows an imam; its collective power corresponds to that imam.
[ELMALILI:1:5#6/r11] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Social spirit precedes the social body, so an individual can carry and represent the conscience of a community before it exists without circularity.
[ELMALILI:1:5#6/r12] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Islam is an unsurpassed social and civil bond; narrow-minded people seek small gods and think restricted brotherhood easier, yet cannot attain a Muslim's firmness and serenity.
[ELMALILI:1:5#6/r13] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The Muslim community's strength depends on the number of its members and the strength of their Islamic conscience; sustaining this universal spirit without an existing community is a prophetic station, especially that of the final Prophet, by divine support.
[ELMALILI:1:5#6/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The breadth and strength of shared feeling set the scale of brotherhood, society, and civilization; narrow particular affiliations fragment wider bonds.
[ELMALILI:1:5#6/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | A community needs both breadth in its common bond and strength in conscience: breadth without strength dissolves it, while strength without breadth prevents its growth.
[ELMALILI:1:5#6/r4] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Social feeling is first a divine innate gift and second a reflection of one's surroundings, and it is shaped by both innate and acquired upbringing.
[ELMALILI:1:5#6/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Only God, without counterpart, equal, or partner, can encompass all human love and fear; devotion to Him grounds universal brotherhood and a worldwide community.
[ELMALILI:1:5#6/r6] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | God trains and strengthens social feeling by taking a covenant from each rational individual in the plural, so each represents all humanity and the worlds.
[ELMALILI:1:5#6/r7] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The first-person plural is grammatically spoken by one individual who represents fellow believers; a congregation speaks through a representative rather than each member saying “I.”
[ELMALILI:1:5#6/r8] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Saying “we worship” makes the individual represent those he feels as brothers, beginning with guardian angels and extending to present or envisaged congregations.
[ELMALILI:1:5#6/r9] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | In the author's school, followers behind the prayer leader recite neither Fatiha nor anything else because the imam recites for them; a person praying alone recites as imam of a potential congregation.
[ELMALILI:1:5#7/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | God first established this covenant in Muhammad's prophetic heart through revelation; he is the complete, truthful servant and representative individual able fully to say the verse, and the model of servanthood.
[ELMALILI:1:5#7/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The faith declaration pairs God's oneness with Muhammad's being His servant and messenger; at Hira the Prophet's worship represented the universal spirit and his communal conscience became imam to all worlds.
[ELMALILI:1:5#7/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Communities sincerely following the Prophet's Sunna can collectively uphold the covenant, submit to no one besides God, and seek aid from no one else; this spirit drove early Islamic conquests and expansion.
[ELMALILI:1:5#7/r4] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Replacing the plural with singular wording in prayer invalidates it because God requires a communal conscience covenant, not an individual-only promise; worshippers should consider whom they represent and on whose behalf they seek aid.
[ELMALILI:1:5#7/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | If no actual worshipping congregation suffices, a Muslim should mentally join the existing congregation to the potential one, including God's angels.
[ELMALILI:1:5#7/r6] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | Exegetes say the plural pronouns refer to the reciter together with guardian angels, the present congregation, or all monotheists.
[ELMALILI:1:5#8/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The verse entails both unity of Lordship, accepting God's unique real essence, and unity of worship, a pledge to form a unified community; the latter builds a relational unity on the former.
[ELMALILI:1:5#8/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The verse renews a witnessed testimony that there is no deity besides God and a commitment to act on it; collective Qur'anic pledges can distribute rights and duties to every individual (an individual obligation) or assign them to the collective body (a communal obligation).
[ELMALILI:1:5#8/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Here the individual sense is retained: each believer bears the individual obligation, while collective testimony is the aggregate of individual testimony; the two consciences mutually guarantee one another.
[ELMALILI:1:5#8/r4] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The verse is pure monotheism and rejects every form of associating partners with God.
[ELMALILI:1:5#8/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · امام فخرالدین رازی | reports | Razi classifies shirk by corporeal versus incorporeal partners: lower or celestial bodies, simple or composite bodies, and material idols, plants, animals, humans, heavenly bodies, or spirits.
[ELMALILI:1:5#8/r6] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · امام فخرالدین رازی | reports | Razi includes worshippers of fire, the sun, moon, stars, and astrologers who attribute fortune and misfortune to the stars, as well as Manichaean light-and-dark dualists.
[ELMALILI:1:5#8/r7] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · امام فخرالدین رازی | reports | Razi describes angel worshippers who assign cosmic and climatic governance to spirits and worship their images, and dualists who posit good and evil first principles such as Yazdan and Ahriman.
[ELMALILI:1:5#8/r8] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | rejects | Two wholly disconnected first principles could not organize one world; if they share kinship or a higher principle, they cease to be first principles, which leads toward the Trinity and Christianity's developed form.
[ELMALILI:1:5#8/r9] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Humanity wandered from awareness of one God into multiplicity, reduced it to two and then Trinity; Islam restores true oneness, and the verse refutes shirk, uniting people who enter Islam while departure fragments and humiliates them.
[ELMALILI:1:5#9/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | After the covenant, the prayer for guidance begins as the most comprehensive practical application of seeking divine aid; it answers the worshipper's need, after pausing at “we seek aid,” to know where and how to begin.
[ELMALILI:1:5#9/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Guidance is contained in seeking aid, which is contained in worship and praise; thus all of Fatiha unfolds as one complete الحمد لله sentence and unified discourse, so its first two pauses are complete but not obligatory.
[ELMALILI:1:5/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Elmalılı renders the verse as worshipping and serving God alone and seeking aid and care from Him alone.
[ELMALILI:1:5/r10] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Intention is a present, created will to obey God and draw near through the act; resolve comes before action, purpose accompanies it, and intention joins knowledge to the act.
[ELMALILI:1:5/r11] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Full awareness, containing both knowledge and will, belongs to the soul and heart.
[ELMALILI:1:5/r12] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Worship also requires an outwardly manifested act of obedience; inward reflection alone may be taat and qurbat but does not become worship.
[ELMALILI:1:5/r13] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Faith requires at least verbal confession as well as inward assent, while an unexpressed inner thought is insufficient as worship.
[ELMALILI:1:5/r14] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | External ritual acts without intention are not worship: sleep is not prayer, hunger is not fasting, giving is not alms, travel is not pilgrimage, and fighting is not jihad.
[ELMALILI:1:5/r15] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | A bad intention, meaning an aim other than obedience and nearness to God, prevents an act from counting as worship.
[ELMALILI:1:5/r16] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | rejects | Turkish tapmak and tapınmak suggest indiscriminate or unconscious obedience and are associated with idols and the cross, so translating worship that way debases the language; kulluk is more aware but weaker than worship.
[ELMALILI:1:5/r17] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Before later legal convention, the shared lexical root meaning of worship should be considered; its broadest sense appears in ubudet or abed and includes worshipper and object of worship.
[ELMALILI:1:5/r18] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Ubudet is the broadest term, while ibadat is narrower; ubudiyet displays humility and ibadat expresses its strongest form, including awe and reverence.
[ELMALILI:1:5/r19] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · cumhûr-i müfessirîn | reports | The majority of exegetes define worship as the utmost degree of humility, which entails complete obedience without asking the reason.
[ELMALILI:1:5/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The imperative meaning 'say this' is implicit; placing the independent pronoun before the verb expresses exclusivity: to You alone, not another.
[ELMALILI:1:5/r20] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · İbn Sikkît | reports | Ibn Sikkit is reported in Abu Hayyan's tafsir as deriving ibadat from the sense of tajrid, or detachment.

rih-i Kāmûs | reports | The commentator on the Qamus says ibadat derives from the root abed, associated with greed or anger.
[ELMALILI:1:5/r22] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | Another explanation says worship is doing what God approves while ubudiyet is being content with what God does; its usage can be narrower or broader, and Prophetic ubudiyet is more specific than ibadat.
[ELMALILI:1:5/r23] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Human life travels between pleasure and pain: fear and hope repeatedly shape action, while despair extinguishes activity and absence of fear leads to transgression and waste.
[ELMALILI:1:5/r24] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Hope needs some fear and fear some hope for a sense of duty; the hungry work to become full and the full work from fear of hunger.
[ELMALILI:1:5/r25] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Human life is an exchange between inner and outer conditions, many of whose causes lie outside us or were not chosen by us; this makes each person sense their own incapacity.
[ELMALILI:1:5/r26] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Even intelligent people cannot escape dependence on hope and fear, and no individual can leave this field of helplessness alone.
[ELMALILI:1:5/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | In legal usage, worship is a special act of obedience that earns reward, depends on intention, and expresses nearness to God.
[ELMALILI:1:5/r4] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Taat is an act rewarded whether or not it depends on intention or the doer knows for whom it is done.
[ELMALILI:1:5/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Qurbat is a rewarded act performed with awareness of the person one seeks to approach, even when intention is not required.
[ELMALILI:1:5/r6] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Every worship act is both qurbat and taat, and every qurbat is taat, but the reverse implications do not hold.
[ELMALILI:1:5/r7] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Reflection to know God is taat but not qurbat while its intended object remains unknown, and without intention it is not worship.
[ELMALILI:1:5/r8] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Qur'an recitation, charity, aid, endowment, and freeing slaves without required intention are qurbat and taat but not ibadat; prayer, fasting, alms, pilgrimage, and jihad with intention are all three.
[ELMALILI:1:5/r9] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Legal worship is conscious obedience and nearness directed only to God through the person's whole spiritual and bodily, outward and inward existence.
[ELMALILI:v1p85/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Elmalılı dedicates his words to God's praise, his heart to God's remembrance, and his own path to God's Book.
[ELMALILI:v1p85/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | He credits God with bringing him into existence and awareness, and with making his heart restless through divine love.
[ELMALILI:v1p85/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | He seeks refuge in God's grace and guidance and asks for mercy because he has failed to worship adequately.
[ELMALILI:v1p85/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Human hearing, speech, and ability to make others love depend on God's enabling; Elmalılı says he cannot do these without God.

[QUTB-ZILAL:1:7/r2] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · رسول الله | reports | Abu Hurayra reports in Sahih Muslim that God calls al-Fatiha a prayer divided between Himself and His servant: praise, mercy, and glorification are the Lord's; worship and aid are shared; guidance and the servant's request belong to the servant, who receives what he asks.

[IBNASHUR:1:5/r11] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The reverse shift appears in Muhammad ibn Bashir al-Khariji’s poem: it opens by addressing someone, then uses a feminine absent pronoun as the addressee seems to shrink from view.

[IBNASHUR:1:5/r14] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · أبو الفتح ابن جني | reports | Ibn Jinni calls iltifāt ‘the bravery of Arabic,’ treating it as evidence of a rhetorician’s agility in directing speech as he wishes.

[IBNASHUR:1:5/r16] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · النحاة | reports | Grammarians variously analyze iyyā as a fixed-form detached pronoun with an emphatic suffix, the pronoun itself followed by clarifying particles, a pronoun support, or a noun annexed to pronouns.
[IBNASHUR:1:5/r17] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Worship ordinarily denotes an act of submission or reverence exceeding what is customary between people; using it for obedience alone is metaphorical.
[IBNASHUR:1:5/r18] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | In religious usage worship is doing what pleases the Lord through submission, compliance, and avoidance, or a morally accountable person’s action against personal desire in reverence for God.

[IBNASHUR:1:5/r32] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Most nations’ worship, including worship prescribed in revealed laws, is founded on love of God; polytheists likewise love their idols as they love God, as 2:165 says. | mentions 2:165

[IBNASHUR:1:5/r37] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The clause ‘and You we ask for help’ is coordinated with worship; it is not separated by the repetition common in supplicatory enumeration, emphasizing that both acts matter under this restriction.

[IBNASHUR:1:5/r4] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · الجمهور من أئمة البلاغة | reports | Most rhetoricians define iltifāt as switching the mode used for the same referent after first expressing it through one of speech, absence, or address.
[IBNASHUR:1:5/r40] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Seeking God’s help means exerting one’s own capacity while asking God to facilitate what a person cannot accomplish alone; this is the religious sense of divine assistance.

[IBNASHUR:1:5/r42] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Nonessential aid provides something that eases an act, such as arranging a mount for someone able to walk; together with necessary aid it completes tawfīq, creating capacity and the impulse to obey.
[IBNASHUR:1:5/r43] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · الراغب | reports | Al-Raghib calls the second, easing kind of aid tawfīq; the author says this does not conflict with scholars’ definition because it follows the necessary aid that first makes tawfīq possible.

[IBNASHUR:1:5/r46] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Knowledge, guidance, revelation, and sciences are also requested aids from God: 90:8–10 points to perception, speech and instruction, and revealed law. | mentions 90:8, 90:9, 90:10

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The names Umm al-Qur'an and Umm al-Kitab are established in the Sunna; “mother” denotes a thing's origin and source.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · عز الدين بن عبد السلام | reports | Ibn Abd al-Salam divides the path to God into outward bodily practice (Sharia) and inward heart practice (Haqiqa), both aiming at servitude as required of the responsible person.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p135/r10] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · النبيء صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A hadith in both Sahihs from Abu Hurayra has God divide prayer between Himself and the servant, answering each portion of al-Fatiha and granting the servant's request. | mentions 1:2, 1:3, 1:4, 1:5, 1:6, 1:7
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p135/r11] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | reports | The verse division differs by region: Medinans exclude the basmala and count “those You favored” as a verse; Meccans and Kufans include the basmala and combine that phrase with its verse; Hasan counts both separately.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p177#2/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · حسان بن ثابت | reports | Al-Isfahani transmits Hassan's story of a poet calling out praise around al-Numan's pavilion; al-Numan recognized al-Nabigha and admitted him, illustrating the Arabic custom of praising a ruler before addressing him.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p177#2/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · الجمهور | reports | Most rhetoricians define iltifat as shifting the same referent among first, second, and third person; al-Sakkaki instead defines it as choosing a person-form other than the contextually apt one.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p177#2/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · السكاكي | reports | Al-Sakkaki counts apostrophe to one's own heart as iltifat, whereas other rhetoricians classify Alqama's example as tajrid; Ibn Ashur explains the difference in their definitions.
